books.eyebrow: Entry the First — Catalogue No. I
books.index_title: Letters written by the late Jonathan Swift, D.D.
books.author: John Hawkesworth, LL.D. (ed.)
subtitle_lines: Dean of St. Patrick's, Dublin; and Several of His Friends
From the Year 1703 to 1740
edition_lines: Published from the Originals, with Notes Explanatory and Historical
books.imprint: Printed for R. Davis, in Piccadilly; T. Davies, in Russel-Street; L. Davis and C. Reymers, in Holborn; and J. Dodsley, in Pall-Mall — London, MDCCLXVI
essay: The letters of Jonathan Swift are among the most revealing documents in the whole of English literature — unguarded dispatches from one of the sharpest minds of the Augustan age, written with no thought for posterity, and all the more vivid for it. This edition, the first substantial collection of Swift's private correspondence, draws on letters spanning nearly four decades, from 1703 to the melancholy silence that descended upon the Dean in his final years. It was published as a companion to Hawkesworth's great collected edition of Swift's Works, the effort of a literary lifetime.

The collection is of particular importance for what it contains of the celebrated Journal to Stella — those intimate, sometimes childlike letters written to Esther Johnson, the woman who remained the central attachment of Swift's life. Hawkesworth edited them with a heavy hand: he suppressed much of the private 'little language,' that idiolect Swift and Stella shared, rendering the letters more presentable to a polite readership whilst stripping them of their most extraordinary quality. Later scholars, examining the manuscripts at the British Museum, would reveal the extent of his interference. The excisions are a loss to literature, though the letters that remain are still among the most companionable ever written.

The correspondence with Pope, Bolingbroke, Gay, Arbuthnot and others illuminates the great literary friendships of the age — the working alliances and warm antagonisms of the Scriblerus Club — seen not in polished essays but in the quick, argumentative, often very funny exchanges of men who genuinely liked one another. Swift writes as he talks: sharp, digressive, tender by turns, and always fiercely intelligent. To read these letters is to sit in the room.

Swift was at this period Dean of St. Patrick's in Dublin — an exile, as he felt it, from the English political world he had briefly inhabited. He had been the most formidable pamphleteer of his age, author of The Conduct of the Allies and a dozen other works that shook governments; the letters show a man who has made his peace with his fate, without ever entirely ceasing to rage against it. Ireland had given him a new cause, and the correspondence bristles with his indignation on behalf of its people.

John Hawkesworth (c.1715–1773), who compiled and annotated this edition, was himself a figure of considerable literary standing. He had succeeded Samuel Johnson as compiler of parliamentary debates for the Gentleman's Magazine, and was a founding contributor to Johnson's Adventurer. His edition of Swift's works, begun in 1754–55, was praised by Johnson himself in the Lives of the Poets. The expanded edition of which these Letters form a part ran eventually to twenty-seven volumes. Hawkesworth would not live to see its completion, dying in 1773 — a death reputedly hastened by the controversy surrounding his account of Captain Cook's voyages, for which he was savagely attacked in the press.
contents: Letters to and from Pope, Gay, Bolingbroke, Arbuthnot and other members of the Scriblerian circle, 1713–1740
Selections from the Journal to Stella (edited by Hawkesworth), 1710–1713
Correspondence concerning Irish affairs and Swift's role as Dean of St. Patrick's, Dublin
Notes Explanatory and Historical by John Hawkesworth, LL.D.

books.eyebrow: Entry the Second — Catalogue No. II
books.index_title: The Works of Alexander Pope — Vol. IV: Satires
books.author: Alexander Pope
title_lines: The Works of Alexander Pope, Esq.
subtitle_lines: Volume the Fourth: Containing the Satires, with their Prologue — the Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot;
and Epilogue — together with the Imitations of Horace
edition_lines: With his Last Corrections, Additions, and Improvements
books.imprint: Printed for C. Bathurst, H. Woodfall, W. Strahan, J. and F. Rivington, and others — London, MDCCLXIX
essay: This fourth volume of the 1769 collected Works gathers the poems upon which Pope's reputation as the great moral voice of his age most securely rests: the Satires, their Prologue in the form of the Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot, the ferocious Epilogue MDCCXXXVIII, and the Imitations of Horace — ten paraphrases of the Roman poet updated with contemporary English reference. Here Pope is at his most combative, most brilliant, and — beneath the armour of wit — most personally revealing.

The Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735) is the masterpiece of the volume: Pope's defence of his life as a satirist, addressed to his dying friend John Arbuthnot, physician and wit. It contains some of the most surgically precise character portraits in the language — the fawning Sporus (Lord Hervey), the envious Atticus (Addison, his face painted with a restraint that makes it all the more cutting). The Imitations of Horace used the stable classical model to attack the specific corruptions of Walpole's England: the venality of court, the decay of taste, the moral torpor of a society growing fat on trade.

Alexander Pope (1688–1744) was the most technically accomplished poet in the English language — a claim that remains, after nearly three centuries, largely uncontested. Born a Roman Catholic in an age when that faith barred its adherents from universities and public office, he was largely self-educated, teaching himself Latin, Greek, French and Italian through the original texts. The technical perfection of his heroic couplets, the density of meaning packed into their paired lines, remains the standard against which all subsequent formal verse in English is measured.

His disability — a curvature of the spine that left him barely four foot six and in constant pain — shaped his temperament. He was sensitive to slight in a way that made enemies readily and kept them permanently. The Dunciad is the monument to his capacity for sustained literary vengeance; the Satires, more compressed, are the evidence that he could wound with the precision of a surgeon's scalpel. He was also, to those he loved — Swift, Gay, the Blount sisters, his mother — a man of extraordinary tenderness.

The 1769 edition represents the standard text of Pope's works as received by the late eighteenth century. Pope, who died twenty-five years before it appeared, had willed his printed works to William Warburton, Bishop of Gloucester, on condition they be published without 'future alterations' — a wish Warburton honoured imperfectly, introducing a handful of changes not sanctioned by any prior edition. This is the quarto edition: a substantial and handsome production, fit for a gentleman's library.
contents: An Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot — being the Prologue to the Satires, 1735
Imitations of Horace — ten paraphrases with contemporary English reference, 1733–38
Epilogue to the Satires, Dialogues I & II — the poems entitled MDCCXXXVIII
Variations from the Author's Manuscripts, and Notes from the Editor's Commentary

books.eyebrow: Entry the Third — Catalogue No. III
books.index_title: The History of England from the Revolution to the Death of George II — Vol. III
books.author: T. Smollett, M.D.
title_lines: from the Revolution to the Death of George II
subtitle_lines: Volume the Third — Designed as a Continuation of Mr. Hume's History
books.imprint: Printed for T. Cadell and R. Baldwin — London, MDCCC
essay: Smollett's History of England is the work of a man who approached the writing of history as he approached the writing of novels: with fierce energy, strong opinions and a determination to make the thing readable. Originally published as a Complete History of England (4 vols., 1757–58) and then continued in a five-volume Continuation (1760–65), it was revised and republished as a complement to David Hume's celebrated earlier history — the two together forming, for decades, the standard popular account of British history from the Norman Conquest to the death of George II in 1760.

Volume III covers the tumultuous middle decades: the reign of George I, the consolidation of the Hanoverian succession, the long domination of Robert Walpole and the developing machinery of parliamentary government that Smollett — a Tory at heart and a Scot by nature — regarded with deep ambivalence. His account of Walpole's ministry vibrates with suppressed contempt that occasionally breaks to the surface; his treatment of the Jacobite rising of 1745 is coloured by his Scottish loyalties, though he was never a Jacobite himself. The prose has the same driving narrative momentum that makes his novels so readable, at the cost of some accuracy and much nuance.

Tobias Smollett (1721–1771) is remembered primarily as a novelist — the author of Roderick Random, Peregrine Pickle, and the masterpiece of his last months, The Expedition of Humphry Clinker. He was the only major eighteenth-century English novelist whose sensibility was genuinely picaresque, shaped by his early years as a naval surgeon and by a ferocious Scottish pride that sat uneasily with the literary world he inhabited. Laurence Sterne caricatured him in the Sentimental Journey as 'Dr. Smelfungus,' travelling everywhere with the spleen. The caricature sticks.

Yet the history shows another Smollett: the industrious professional writer, capable of sustained scholarly effort, reading voraciously and synthesising material across decades and reigns. He edited the Critical Review, translated Cervantes, wrote plays and poems and political journalism — all while producing novels and this substantial history. He was, in the language of the trade, a hack in the best sense: a writer who could do anything, quickly, and usually well. He died of tuberculosis near Livorno in 1771, having finished Humphry Clinker only months before. Charles Dickens, one of his great admirers, visited his grave.

The partnership of Smollett and Hume — neither of whom the other particularly liked — gave the reading public of the late eighteenth century its standard account of British history. Smollett brings to his portion exactly what Hume brings to his: a powerful organising intelligence, a strong point of view, and the ability to make the past feel urgent. The history is no longer read as history; it is still read, by those who find it, with considerable pleasure.
contents: The Hanoverian Succession and the reign of George I, 1714–1727
The era of Walpole — the rise and fall of the first Prime Minister
The War of Austrian Succession and British foreign policy, 1740s
The Jacobite Rising of 1745 and its aftermath

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fourth — Catalogue No. IV
books.index_title: Novels and Tales of the Author of Waverley — Vol. IV: The Antiquary
books.author: Sir Walter Scott
title_lines: Novels and Tales of the Author of Waverley
subtitle_lines: Volume the Fourth: The Antiquary
edition_lines: By the Author of Waverley, Guy Mannering, &c.
books.imprint: Printed by James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co., Edinburgh; and Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, London — MDCCCXIX
essay: The Antiquary is the third of the Waverley novels and the one its author loved best. Scott said so himself, and the affection is visible on every page: this is the novel in which he is most at ease, most humorous, most deeply invested in the texture of ordinary Scottish life. The title character, Jonathan Oldbuck of Monkbarns — amateur historian, archaeologist and collector of items of sometimes doubtful antiquity — is the closest thing Scott ever wrote to a self-portrait. Like Scott, Oldbuck is possessed by the past; like Scott, he is more comfortable with the dead than with many of the living.

The novel is set in the last decade of the eighteenth century, in a small Scottish coastal community, and its central comedy springs from Oldbuck's passionate, magnificently unreliable scholarship. In one celebrated scene, the local beggar Edie Ochiltree demolishes Oldbuck's proudest antiquarian discovery, the supposed Roman praetorium on his land, with the breezy testimony of a man who helped build it. The scene is both very funny and quietly devastating. H. J. C. Grierson wrote that few writers, apart from Shakespeare, could blend truth and poetry, realism and romance, more wonderfully than Scott does here.

The 1819 edition presented here is one of the collected Novels and Tales of the Author of Waverley, produced in Edinburgh by Archibald Constable — the publisher who backed Scott's great literary enterprise from its anonymous beginnings in 1814. The authorship of the Waverley novels was one of the most elaborately maintained literary secrets of the age: Scott did not publicly acknowledge the books until 1827, and the title pages of all editions before that date bear only the formula 'By the Author of Waverley.' The secret was widely guessed and widely known, but the pretence was maintained with remarkable consistency, partly for tax reasons, partly from Scott's genuine pleasure in the game.

The plot is more loosely constructed than either Waverley or Guy Mannering, and Scott knew it. The love interest — the mysterious Lovel and the genteel Isabella Wardour — is handled perfunctorily, and the novel's conclusion was judged abrupt even by contemporary readers. But these are the cavils of those who are looking in the wrong direction. The Antiquary is not really a plot novel; it is a world novel, and the world it creates — the harbour town, the fishermen's cottages, the antiquary's cluttered study, the great rescue scene on the flooding sands — has a completeness and solidity that no amount of plot engineering could supply.

Walter Scott (1771–1832), born in Edinburgh and raised partly in the Border country he would make famous, had already established himself as the most popular poet in Britain when he turned to prose fiction. The Waverley novels were among the most widely read books in Europe for most of the nineteenth century, and their influence on the historical novel — on Dumas, Hugo, Manzoni, Tolstoy — was incalculable. He was made a baronet in 1820, the year after this edition was published. Six years later, financial catastrophe — the collapse of his publisher Constable — left him with debts of over £100,000. He resolved to write them off rather than declare bankruptcy. He very nearly succeeded, dying at his beloved Abbotsford in 1832.
contents: Jonathan Oldbuck of Monkbarns — the Antiquary, amateur scholar and collector
Edie Ochiltree — licensed beggar, keeper of local memory and demolisher of illusions
Lovel (Major Neville) — the young stranger of obscure birth, and his pursuit of Isabella Wardour
Sir Arthur Wardour — an ancient baronet beset by debt and ancestral pride

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifth — Catalogue No. V
books.index_title: The Monastery: A Romance
books.author: Sir Walter Scott, Bart.
subtitle_lines: A Romance — By the Author of Waverley
books.imprint: Printed for Archibald Constable and Co. and John Ballantyne, Bookseller to the King, Edinburgh; and Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, London — MDCCCXX
essay: The Monastery was written at breakneck speed in the autumn and winter of 1819, largely while the printing of Ivanhoe was stalled for want of paper. Scott began it in August 1819, had the third volume at press by the end of February 1820, and published it on 23 March of that year. It is set in the Scottish Border country of the 1550s, at the moment when the Reformation is beginning to crack the old Catholic order, and its action revolves around the fictional monastery of Kennaquhair — almost certainly modelled on the great Cistercian abbey of Melrose, just a few miles from Scott's own estate at Abbotsford. Scott knew this landscape in his bones.

The central drama is both historical and domestic. Father Eustace, the scholarly sub-prior devoted to the defence of the old faith, finds himself opposed by a Protestant preacher — Henry Warden — who had once been his intimate friend at college. Around them, the Avenel and Glendinning families are entangled: the Glendinning brothers, Halbert and Edward, both fall in love with Mary Avenel, and the divergence of their fates — Halbert into the world, Edward into the cloister — traces the novel's larger argument about the rival claims of the active and contemplative life. The Reformation, for Scott, is presented not as triumph or tragedy but as transformation: the inevitable passing of one world into another, with its full measure of loss and gain.

The novel is remembered — not always fondly — for its most ambitious invention: the White Lady of Avenel, a supernatural spirit who speaks only in verse and intervenes at crucial moments to alter the course of events. Scott was drawing on German Romantic sources, particularly Friedrich de la Motte Fouque's tale of the water nymph Undine, and on Celtic mythological tradition. The White Lady was not popular with readers, and Scott himself, writing the preface for the 1830 Magnum edition, conceded the failure with characteristic candour: the character was, he admitted, neither sufficiently human to engage the emotions nor sufficiently supernatural to command awe.

Contemporary reviews were mixed: the landscape descriptions were generally admired, as were the scenes of religious conflict between Eustace and Warden, but the overall construction was judged inferior to its predecessors. Scott himself agreed. Yet the novel continued to sell. As he observed in that same preface, literary reputation is seldom built in a single effort, and rarely lost by a solitary miscarriage. The Monastery was followed immediately by its sequel, The Abbot — also published in 1820, in what was one of the most remarkable years of literary production in the history of English fiction.

This first edition — published on 23 March 1820 — is the only Scott publication in which his printer John Ballantyne used the title 'Bookseller to the King' in the imprint, a bibliographical distinction noted by Todd and Bowden. Scott had been awarded his baronetcy that same year. He was at the height of his powers and his fame, master of Abbotsford, the most popular novelist in Europe. Within five years the financial catastrophe would begin that would consume the rest of his life. This volume belongs to the brief, gilded moment before.
contents: Father Eustace — sub-prior of Kennaquhair, devoted defender of the old Catholic faith
Halbert and Edward Glendinning — two brothers divided by temperament, faith and love
Mary Avenel — ward of Dame Elspeth, beloved by both brothers, companion of the White Lady
The White Lady of Avenel — spirit of ambiguous nature who speaks only in verse
Sir Piercie Shafton — Elizabethan courtier, refugee from England, and comic euphuist

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixth — Catalogue No. VI
books.index_title: Charles O'Malley, the Irish Dragoon
books.author: Charles James Lever
subtitle_lines: In Two Volumes — Edited by Harry Lorrequer
books.imprint: Published by William Curry, Jun. and Company, Dublin; W. S. Orr and Company, London — MDCCCXLI. With Illustrations on Steel by Phiz (Hablot Knight Browne)
essay: Charles O'Malley is the novel that made Lever's name — a rollicking, headlong, thoroughly Irish picaresque following its reckless young hero from the drawing rooms of Galway through the carnage of the Peninsular War and finally to Waterloo, where he watches the great battle from the wrong side of the field. It was serialised in monthly parts between March 1840 and December 1841, illustrated throughout by Phiz (Hablot Knight Browne), who was simultaneously illustrating three works by Dickens — and the strain occasionally shows, Lever himself noting that Phiz's O'Malley figures were beginning to look suspiciously like his Pickwick and Nickleby figures.

The novel was Lever's second, following The Confessions of Harry Lorrequer (1839), and it confirmed his position as the foremost Irish popular novelist of his generation — an author whose sales rivalled those of Dickens and Thackeray in the early 1840s. Its central character, the impudent, high-spirited O'Malley, is drawn from real Dublin originals, as is his immortal comic servant Mickey Free, described by Lever as 'a composite of several droll grooms.' The set-piece scenes — the wild fox hunt that opens the novel, the Peninsular sieges, the bivouacs and balls of the retreat — have the breathless energy of a man writing faster than he can think, which is substantially what Lever was doing.

Charles James Lever (1806–1872) was born in Dublin of English parents, trained as a physician, practised medicine in the west of Ireland during the cholera epidemic of 1832, and spent years writing fiction in Brussels before returning to Dublin in 1842 to edit the Dublin University Magazine. He was acquainted with Thackeray, who dedicated The Irish Sketch Book to him, and with Dickens. He is best remembered for his early military and sporting novels, though his later work — darker, more introspective, shaped by years of continental exile — has found increasing appreciation. He spent his final years as British consul in Trieste.

The collaboration with Phiz was artistically productive but logistically fraught. Lever was often late with copy; a fire at the printer's office destroyed one manuscript; and Phiz was so overcommitted that the illustrations occasionally recycled poses from other projects. The novel was first published in Dublin by William Curry, with simultaneous London publication by W. S. Orr — a common arrangement for Irish books of the period seeking metropolitan distribution. An American edition appeared simultaneously from Carey and Hart of Philadelphia, a measure of the novel's transatlantic appeal.

A widow wrote to Lever's brother to say that the novel had transformed her nervous, timid son — who had been given a place at Woolwich but hesitated to take it — inspiring him with 'a passion for movement and adventure, and spiriting him to an eager desire for a military life.' Lever recalled the letter with pleasure for the rest of his career. He reprinted it in the preface to a later edition, along with the observation — written from Trieste in 1872, a few months before his death — that whatever he had done well subsequently, he owed the public's patience for it to the popularity of this book.
contents: Vol. I — Galway and Dublin: the fox hunt, Daly's Club-house, and O'Malley's departure for the wars
Vol. II — The Peninsular Campaign: sieges, retreats, and the friendship with Frank Webber
The Battle of Waterloo: O'Malley in the French camp and on the field
Mickey Free — comic servant, irrepressible Irishman, and the novel's most memorable creation
Illustrations by Phiz (Hablot Knight Browne): 42 plates across two volumes

books.eyebrow: Entry the Seventh — Catalogue No. VII
books.index_title: Our Mess — Vol. II: Tom Burke of Ours
books.author: Charles James Lever
subtitle_lines: Tom Burke of 'Ours'
edition_lines: Charles James Lever — Edited by Harry Lorrequer
books.imprint: Published by William Curry, Jun. and Company, Dublin — MDCCCXLIV. With Illustrations on Steel by Phiz
essay: Tom Burke is the most ambitiously conceived of Lever's early novels and the most structurally eccentric. Its publication history is itself a bibliographical curiosity: issued as Volumes II and III of a three-volume series under the collective title Our Mess (Volume I having been Jack Hinton, the Guardsman, published in 1843), it also exists as an independent two-volume work with its own title pages, binding, and identity. The running heads on the left read 'Our Mess' and on the right 'Tom Burke of Ours' — a compromise that satisfied no one but accurately reflected the publishing situation.

The novel follows Tom Burke, an Irish orphan of good family cheated of his inheritance by a rascally attorney, from Dublin through the revolutionary underground of 1798 and across the Channel to France, where he rises through the ranks of Napoleon's army. Napoleon himself appears — a device Lever had employed briefly in O'Malley but here develops with greater ambition. The Emperor is portrayed with a mixture of awe and disenchantment that reflects Lever's own complicated feelings about heroism and power: admirable as a military genius, troubling as an autocrat. Volume II, which is the book in this library, takes up Burke's story at the height of the Napoleonic campaigns.

The serialisation ran in the Dublin University Magazine from February 1843 through September 1844 — twenty parts in all, the final double number being dated from Templeogue House by 'Harry Lorrequer' on 25 August 1844. Lever was simultaneously editing the magazine, seeing patients, corresponding with Thackeray, and attempting to raise a family. The strain is occasionally visible in the novel's construction, which is looser and more digressive than O'Malley. Lever himself later acknowledged the difficulties the material had caused him.

Charles James Lever (1806–1872) shared with Dickens not only an illustrator (Phiz), a publisher (Chapman and Hall handled later editions), and a readership, but also a fascination with the way institutions — armies, courts, prisons, clubs — shape and deform the individuals trapped within them. His Irish perspective on the Napoleonic Wars — sympathetic to France, contemptuous of English policy in Ireland, alert to the absurdities of military hierarchy — gives Tom Burke a satirical edge that his earlier novels largely lack.

The first edition was printed in Dublin and bound either in the original serial wrappers or in rose-madder ribbed cloth — a newer style of binding that Sadleir notes as characteristic of the 1840s. Forty-four plates by Phiz are present across the two volumes. The novel was reprinted by Chapman and Hall in London in 1865, two decades after its first appearance, by which time Lever had moved decisively away from the rollicking style of his early career toward the more sombre psychological fiction of his maturity.
contents: Vol. II — Tom Burke as officer in Napoleon's army: the campaigns and their human cost
Napoleon Bonaparte as a character: admired general, troubling autocrat
The subplot of inheritance and legal villainy: Basset, Crofts, and the Burke estates
Minette the vivandiere: the novel's romantic centre in the Peninsular chaos
44 illustrations by Phiz across the two volumes of Our Mess

books.eyebrow: Entry the Eighth — Catalogue No. VIII
books.index_title: Q. Horatius Flaccus — Recensuit Io. Casp. Orellius
books.author: Johann Caspar von Orelli
subtitle_lines: Recensuit atque Interpretatus est Io. Casp. Orellius — Editio Altera Emendatior
edition_lines: Tomus Decimus — Johann Caspar von Orelli
books.imprint: Sumptibus Orellii Fuesslini et Sociorum — Turici [Zurich], MDCCCXLIII–XLIV
essay: This is one of the monuments of nineteenth-century classical scholarship: Orelli's edition of the complete works of Horace, revised and expanded in this second edition, printed in Zurich by the house of Orell Fussli. The full title announces that Orelli has 'reviewed and interpreted' the text — recensuit atque interpretatus est — a formula that accurately describes his dual achievement: a critically established Latin text and an exegetical commentary drawing on all significant prior scholarship, synthesised with what the Encyclopaedia Britannica called 'great taste and extensive learning.' The edition runs to two thick octavo volumes, the text presented in double column, bristling with annotation.

Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC) is the supreme lyric poet of Latin literature — an achievement made more remarkable by the improbability of his life. Born the son of a freed slave in Venusia in southern Italy, he was sent by his father at considerable personal sacrifice to be educated in Rome and then Athens; he fought on the losing side at Philippi under Brutus; and he emerged from the ruins of the Republic to become the most celebrated poet of the Augustan age, intimate of Maecenas and of Augustus himself. His Odes attempt, and largely achieve, the transposition into Latin of the metres and spirit of Pindar and Alcaeus; his Satires and Epistles invented a conversational verse whose influence runs through Pope, Dryden and Johnson.

Johann Caspar von Orelli (1787–1849) was born in Zurich of an Italian Protestant family that had sought refuge in Switzerland at the Reformation — a family history that gave him early access to both Italian literature and Reformed theology. He worked as a preacher in Bergamo from 1807 to 1814, acquiring the taste for Italian letters that coloured his subsequent scholarship. Returning to Switzerland, he became professor of eloquence and hermeneutics at the Carolinum in Zurich and later at the new University of Zurich, the foundation of which was largely due to his own efforts. He was by every account a man of liberal temper: a supporter of Greek independence, a champion of popular education, and a teacher of extraordinary power.

His three great scholarly works were his edition of Cicero in eight volumes (1826–38), this edition of Horace (first published 1837–38, revised here in 1843–44), and the Inscriptionum Latinarum Selectarum Collectio (1828), a collection of Latin inscriptions that remains a standard reference. The Horace was the most widely used critical edition of the poet in European universities throughout the mid-nineteenth century, and its influence persisted long after Orelli's death in 1849. A fourth edition appeared as late as 1886–92, revised by other hands.

To hold this volume is to hold the working instrument of Victorian classical education — the text from which schoolmasters across Britain and the Continent taught their pupils to construe the Odes and to decline the infinitives of the Epistles. The margins of surviving copies are frequently thick with the annotations of successive readers, each generation making its own argument with Orelli's choices. The edition is, in the deepest sense, a conversation — between editor and poet, between scholar and student, between the ancient world and all subsequent ages that have tried to understand it.
contents: The complete works of Horace: Odes (4 books), Epodes, Carmen Saeculare, Satires, Epistles, Ars Poetica
Orelli's critical apparatus: variant readings from manuscripts and prior editions
Exegetical commentary: interpretations drawn from Renaissance and Enlightenment scholarship
Index of proper names, geographical references, and metrical analysis

books.eyebrow: Entry the Ninth — Catalogue No. IX
books.index_title: Annals of Horticulture and Year Book of Practical Gardening
books.author: George Glenny et al.
title_lines: and Year Book of Information on Practical Gardening
subtitle_lines: For the Year 1848 — The Third Annual Volume
edition_lines: Anonymous — Principal Contributions by George Glenny
books.imprint: Published by Charles Cox — London, MDCCCXLVIII. With a Hand-Coloured Lithograph Frontispiece by James Andrews and Wood-Engraved Illustrations
essay: The Annals of Horticulture was a short-lived but substantial annual publication that appeared between 1846 and 1850, each volume a comprehensive record of the year's developments in garden flowers, fruit culture, and horticultural practice. This third volume for 1848 runs to nearly six hundred pages and is decorated with a hand-coloured lithograph frontispiece by James Andrews, one of the period's most accomplished flower painters, alongside numerous wood-engraved illustrations in the text. The editorship was officially anonymous, but a large portion of the articles — particularly a series of short monographs on individual flowers — were contributed by George Glenny, the opinionated and prolific horticultural writer whose strident opinions about what constituted a perfect florist's flower were a constant source of controversy in the gardening press.

Eighteen forty-eight was an extraordinary year in European history — the year of revolutions, of Chartism, of the Communist Manifesto — and to open a substantial volume of gardening instruction and flower portraiture is to be reminded of how completely the Victorian educated class maintained its inner life of cultivation and order alongside the upheavals of the public world. The volume covers garden flowers in exhaustive detail (roses, dahlias, chrysanthemums, auriculas, carnations and pinks receive particular attention), along with sections on kitchen gardens, fruit trees, greenhouse management, and the increasingly popular practice of bedding out tender plants.

George Glenny (1793–1874) was the most combative personality in Victorian popular horticulture — a man whose certainty about the proper form of a florist's tulip or the ideal shape of a dahlia flower was matched only by his enthusiasm for public argument. He edited or contributed to several horticultural periodicals over a long career, and his standards for what constituted a perfect specimen flower were precise, dogmatic and frequently disputed. His monographs in this volume on individual flower types preserve a snapshot of mid-Victorian floristry at its most confident and opinionated.

The 1848 volume also contains articles on landscape design and garden architecture — a reflection of the growing Victorian interest in the designed garden as an extension of domestic space — and on the management of conservatories and greenhouses, which were becoming established features of prosperous Victorian households by mid-century. John Claudius Loudon's influence, though he had died in 1843, is everywhere visible in the scope and ambition of the coverage: the idea that the educated gardener should command not just practical technique but botanical and aesthetic principle.

The Annals of Horticulture was published from Charles Cox's premises in London, though earlier volumes had been issued by Houlston and Stoneman. It ceased publication after the 1850 volume, having achieved five annual numbers — a short run that was nonetheless sufficient to establish it as a useful record of Victorian horticultural practice at the height of the bedding-out era, when the English garden was being transformed by the availability of greenhouse-raised tender perennials and the ambitions of a newly prosperous reading public.

Greenhouse and conservatory management: the new fashion for tender plants

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Third & Sixty-Fourth — Catalogue No. LXIII–LXIV
books.index_title: Theodor Körners sämmtliche Werke (Vols. I & III of IV)
books.author: Theodor Körner
subtitle_lines: In Vier Bänden — the First and Third Volumes
Erster Band: Dramatische Beiträge — Dritter Band: Zriny und Rosamunde
edition_lines: A Posthumous Collected Edition of the Poet-Soldier
Printed in the Old German Letter
books.imprint: Published at Stuttgart — undated, in the German nineteenth century [s.a.]
essay: These two volumes belong to a collected edition of the works of Theodor Körner, the young German poet who became, after his early death in the wars against Napoleon, one of the abiding romantic figures of the nineteenth century. The set was issued in four volumes under the old title Theodor Körners sämmtliche Werke; the present library holds the first and the third. Volume I gathers the Dramatische Beiträge, the dramatic pieces Körner wrote for the Vienna stage; Volume III contains his two tragedies, Zriny and Rosamunde. They are handsome, sober German volumes, printed in the old black-letter type, and they carry the unmistakable seriousness with which the nineteenth century treated its national poets.

Körner's life reads like the libretto of a Romantic opera, and was treated as such almost at once. Born in Dresden in 1791, the son of Christian Gottfried Körner — Schiller's closest friend — he grew up in the warmth of German classicism, wrote light comedies and then ambitious tragedies for the Vienna Burgtheater, and made his name overnight with Zriny in 1812. When the war of liberation against Napoleon broke out he threw it all over, enlisted in the Lützow Free Corps, and was killed in a skirmish near Gadebusch in August 1813, aged twenty-one. His battle-songs, published by his grieving father as Leyer und Schwert, made him a martyr and a symbol; Weber and Schubert set them to music, and generations of German schoolboys learned them by heart.

The two volumes here give the dramatist rather than the soldier-poet. Zriny, the centrepiece of Volume III, dramatises the historical defence of the fortress of Szigetvár in 1566, where the Croatian-Hungarian commander Nikola Zrinski died holding the walls against the Ottomans — a subject Körner turned into a hymn to patriotic self-sacrifice that audiences received as a coded call to resist Napoleon. Rosamunde is the slighter companion tragedy, and Volume I's dramatic pieces show the lighter, more theatrical talent of his Vienna years. The famous war-songs of Leyer und Schwert, it should be said, are not in these volumes — they belong to the absent Volume IV — so what the library holds is the playwright, with the legend kept just offstage.

The edition itself is undated. This is not unusual: nineteenth-century German publishers reprinted their classic authors so continuously that many editions carry no year at all, and Körner, endlessly reissued, was among the most reprinted of them. The imprint gives only Stuttgart — which is to say a great deal, for Stuttgart was the capital of German classics publishing, the city of Cotta, who printed Goethe and Schiller. The 'sämmtliche' spelling and the black-letter type place the book firmly in the nineteenth century without pinning it to a single year; an honest catalogue records it as undated rather than guessing. Körner's later afterlife was a complicated one — his image as the poet who died for the fatherland was taken up by every subsequent wave of German nationalism, and put to uses he could not have foreseen — but the volumes themselves are simply the work of a gifted young writer, preserved with the care his countrymen gave their dead.

A German voice sits well in this library, beside the French of Montalembert, Faguet and Dumas, the Latin of the Horace, and the Irish thread that runs throughout: it widens the collection's conversation across the European nineteenth century. And there is a particular fitness in an undated, anonymous-looking Stuttgart reprint of a poet who died at twenty-one. The grand collected edition, the black-letter dignity, the missing volumes — all of it speaks of the way a culture keeps its young dead alive by printing them, over and over, long after the particular occasion of their fame has passed. That is, in the end, what this whole library is about.
contents: Volume I — Dramatische Beiträge: the dramatic pieces written for the Vienna Burgtheater
Volume III — Zriny: a tragedy on the defence of Szigetvár (1566) and patriotic sacrifice
Volume III — Rosamunde: a tragedy
The poet's life: Dresden 1791 — fallen with the Lützow Free Corps, 1813, aged twenty-one
Published at Stuttgart, undated; the war-songs of Leyer und Schwert belong to the absent Volume IV

books.index_title: Robertson's Ecclesiastical Reports — Volume II
books.author: James Robertson
subtitle_lines: Volume the Second — Reports of Cases decided in the Arches and Prerogative Courts of Canterbury, and in the High Court of Delegates
edition_lines: James Robertson, Esq., of Doctors' Commons
books.imprint: Published by V. & R. Stevens and G. S. Norton — London, MDCCCLIII
essay: Robertson's Ecclesiastical Reports is precisely what its title announces: a systematic record of cases heard before the Arches Court of Canterbury and the Prerogative Court, together with decisions of the High Court of Delegates — the principal appellate tribunal in ecclesiastical matters before its jurisdiction was transferred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in 1832. These courts handled the matters that touched the Church of England's boundaries with civil society: probate of wills, questions of marriage validity, disputes over church property, and the discipline of the clergy. In an age before the full secularisation of English law, they occupied a significant position in the legal landscape.

The Arches Court — so called from its former location in the church of St Mary-le-Bow, whose arched crypt gave the court its name — was the principal ecclesiastical court of the Province of Canterbury, hearing appeals from the diocesan courts below. Doctors' Commons, the collegiate body of civil and ecclesiastical lawyers who practised before it, was a world unto itself, occupying a quadrangle near St Paul's Cathedral and conducting its affairs in Latin and in the traditions of Roman canon law. Dickens caricatured it in David Copperfield; it was abolished in 1857, just four years after this volume appeared.

Volume II covers cases from the 1840s and early 1850s — a period of considerable ecclesiastical controversy in England, when the Oxford Movement, the Gorham judgment (1850), and disputes over church ritual were generating a stream of litigation that tested the boundaries of the established Church's authority. The Gorham case in particular — which turned on whether the Privy Council could overrule the Bishop of Exeter on a question of baptismal regeneration — convulsed the Church and prompted several prominent figures, including Henry Edward Manning, to convert to Rome. The reports provide a dry but revealing record of these currents.

James Robertson practised as an advocate at Doctors' Commons and compiled these reports from cases he had personally argued or observed. The tradition of law reporting in this specialist area was thin and imperfect; Robertson's volumes represent a systematic attempt to provide the ecclesiastical bar with a reliable record of precedent. The standard of the reporting is professional and economical: headnotes summarising the legal issues, followed by full accounts of the arguments and the judgments, with references to earlier authority.

There is something quietly poignant about a book of ecclesiastical law reports published in 1853, just four years before the institution it served — Doctors' Commons and the Arches Court in its old form — was swept away by the reforming legislation of 1857. The volume is a fossil of a legal world that had endured, in its essentials, since the Middle Ages: the world of canon law, of the civilian tradition, of advocates arguing in Latin before judges who wore scarlet robes and sat beneath the arms of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Within a decade, all of it would be gone.
contents: Cases from the Arches Court of Canterbury: discipline, property, and the limits of ecclesiastical jurisdiction
Prerogative Court cases: probate of wills and questions of testamentary capacity
High Court of Delegates: appellate decisions in the years before the Privy Council assumed jurisdiction
The Gorham controversy and its legal aftermath, 1850–52
Index of cases reported; table of authorities cited

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twelfth — Catalogue No. XII
books.index_title: Executive Documents, 1st Session, 33rd Congress — Vol. I, Part III
books.author: United States House of Representatives
title_lines: Executive Documents of the First Session
subtitle_lines: Volume the First, Part the Third — House of Representatives
edition_lines: Presented by Order of the Congress of the United States of America
books.imprint: Printed by A. O. P. Nicholson, Public Printer — Washington, City of Washington, MDCCCLIV
essay: The executive documents of the 33rd Congress, first session (1853–54), represent one of the most consequential legislative moments in American history. The 33rd Congress was presided over by President Franklin Pierce, a Northern Democrat who had won the presidency on a platform of sectional compromise; its first session would culminate in the passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act of May 1854, which repealed the Missouri Compromise of 1820, opened the new territories to popular sovereignty on the question of slavery, and ignited the chain of events — Bleeding Kansas, the collapse of the Whig party, the formation of the Republican party, and ultimately the Civil War — that would determine the fate of the nation.

This third part of the first volume of executive documents contains the reports, correspondence, and official communications submitted by the executive branch to the House of Representatives during the session — the raw material of government: dispatches from foreign ministers, army and navy reports, returns from federal land offices, communications from the Treasury, reports on Indian affairs and territorial governance. It is the documentary sediment of empire at its most administrative — the paperwork of a continental republic stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, managing territories acquired from France and Mexico and contested with Britain.

The documents reflect the vast ambitions of mid-century American expansion: surveys of potential railroad routes to the Pacific (the Pacific Railroad Surveys were being conducted simultaneously), reports on the newly organised territories of Washington, Oregon, and Utah, and the continuing correspondence on Central American affairs that reflected American anxiety about British influence in the region. The Gadsden Purchase — by which the United States acquired from Mexico the strip of territory that now forms southern Arizona and New Mexico, specifically to provide a southern route for a transcontinental railroad — was being negotiated during precisely this session and is reflected in the diplomatic papers.

The 33rd Congress was also the Congress in which debate over the Kansas-Nebraska bill consumed and eventually destroyed the existing political alignments of the republic. Stephen Douglas, who introduced the bill, believed that popular sovereignty would settle the slavery question peacefully; its opponents — Salmon Chase, Charles Sumner, and the young Abraham Lincoln, who had retired to private practice but was galvanised back into politics by the Act's passage — believed, correctly, that it would only inflame it. The executive documents record the legislative machinery of the period, with no awareness of the catastrophe they are helping to prepare.

That a volume of American congressional documents should find its way into an Irish antiquarian library is itself a small historical curiosity — perhaps acquired by a traveller, or received from an American correspondent, or purchased from the stock of a Dublin book dealer who had obtained it with a lot of miscellaneous papers. It is not a book that anyone read for pleasure; it is a book that accumulates meaning from what surrounds it in history, a bureaucratic document that sits, innocently, at the edge of an abyss.
contents: Foreign affairs correspondence: relations with Britain, France, and the Central American states
Army and Navy reports: the Pacific Railroad Surveys and western territorial management
Indian Affairs: reports from the Bureau and from territorial governors
Treasury returns and Land Office reports: the fiscal machinery of continental expansion
The Gadsden Purchase negotiations: the southern transcontinental railroad route

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirteenth — Catalogue No. XIII
books.index_title: The Chemistry of Common Life — Volume I
books.author: James F. W. Johnston, F.R.S.
subtitle_lines: Volume the First
edition_lines: James Finlay Weir Johnston, F.R.S., F.G.S., Reader in Chemistry and Mineralogy in the University of Durham
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London; D. Appleton and Company, New York — MDCCCLV
essay: Johnston's Chemistry of Common Life is one of the finest works of Victorian popular science — a book that set out to demonstrate that chemistry was not a laboratory abstraction but the hidden grammar of daily life: the process by which air feeds the blood, water sustains the cell, soil yields the harvest, food becomes energy, and narcotics alter consciousness. Beginning with food and drink and proceeding through poisons, scents, narcotics, fertilisers and explosives, it led its readers into thinking chemically about a world they had always taken for granted. The first volume serialised from 1853, with individual parts selling between five thousand and thirty thousand copies — extraordinary figures for a work of serious popular science.

Johnston was peculiarly equipped for the enterprise. A fellow of the Royal Society, a founder of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, a reader in chemistry at Durham, and the foremost authority on agricultural chemistry in Britain, he had spent his career arguing that chemistry was the fundamental science of practical life — of farming, of industry, of public health. His earlier Lectures on Agricultural Chemistry and Geology (1842) and Catechism of Agricultural Chemistry (1844) had reached wide audiences; The Chemistry of Common Life was the summation of his ambition to make chemistry available to any educated reader, regardless of scientific training.

Nature's review, published some years after Johnston's death, recalled the 'keen interest and pleasure' the book had awakened in the reviewer as a boy, and judged that no subsequent flood of scientific manuals and primers had superseded it: it was 'full of facts which it is often difficult to find elsewhere, written in a style which will charm the most fastidious.' This was the achievement Johnston had aimed at: to make chemistry not merely comprehensible but interesting, to show that the most ordinary domestic and natural phenomena — the browning of meat in a pan, the rising of bread, the heating effect of whisky, the narcotic action of opium — were expressions of the same universal principles.

James Finlay Weir Johnston (1796–1855) was born in Kilmarnock, worked his way through Glasgow University by tutoring, won prizes in both science and humanities, visited the great Swedish chemist Berzelius in 1829, and built his career in the new and stringently Anglican University of Durham from 1833 onwards — as a dissenter, always slightly at odds with the institution he served. He was a man of broad curiosity and genuine literary gifts, dedicated to the proposition that science was not the property of specialists. He died of a lung infection contracted abroad in 1855, the year his masterpiece was published, and did not live to see its success.

The book was revised after Johnston's death by George Henry Lewes — the philosopher, critic, and companion of George Eliot — and remained in print into the late nineteenth century. It was translated into Dutch, Chinese, and other languages; the Dutch translation was used as a textbook in primary schools and for self-study among workers and farmers, suggesting the breadth of the audience Johnston had always intended to reach. To hold the first edition of Volume I is to hold the moment before the book became an institution: the fresh, ambitious, slightly improbable thing it was before success confirmed it.
contents: The air we breathe: nitrogen, oxygen, and carbonic acid — their roles in sustaining life
The water we drink: analysis, purification, and the chemistry of aqueous solutions
The plants we rear: photosynthesis, soil chemistry, and the basis of agricultural productivity
The food we eat: the chemistry of digestion, nutrition, and the transformation of organic matter
Narcotics, stimulants, and poisons: the chemistry of substances that alter the body and the mind

books.eyebrow: Entry the Tenth — Catalogue No. X
books.index_title: The Life of Robert, First Lord Clive
books.author: Rev. G. R. Gleig
title_lines: The Life of Robert, First Lord Clive
edition_lines: By the Rev. G. R. Gleig, M.A., Chaplain-General to the Forces
books.imprint: Published by John Murray, Albemarle Street — London, MDCCCLVIII
essay: Robert Clive (1725–1774) is one of the most dramatic and most contested figures in the history of British India — the man who, more than any other, converted the East India Company from a trading house into a territorial power. His victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, achieved with a force of barely 3,000 against Siraj ud-Daulah's fifty thousand, established British supremacy in Bengal. His administration of Bengal, ruthless in its pursuit of Company profits, sowed the conditions for the famine of 1770 that would kill millions. He defended himself before Parliament with the famous declaration that he stood astonished at his own moderation. He died by his own hand in 1774, aged forty-nine.

George Robert Gleig (1796–1888) was peculiarly well qualified to write a military biography. He had served as a lieutenant in the Peninsular War — present at the siege of San Sebastian, the battles of the Nivelle and the Nive, wounded three times — and then in the American War of 1812, where he took part in the capture of Washington. After Waterloo he returned to Oxford, took orders, and became one of the most prolific writers on military subjects in Victorian Britain: historian, biographer, and eventually Chaplain-General to the Forces. His biography of Clive, published by John Murray in 1858, draws on family papers and official correspondence to give a sympathetic but not uncritical account of its subject.

Gleig approached Clive as a soldier would: with admiration for the audacity of Plassey and the subsequent reorganisation of Bengal, and with a soldier's instinctive sympathy for a man who had to make decisions under pressure that the comfortable armchair critic could always second-guess from safety. The Parliamentary inquiry of 1772–73 — in which Clive's conduct was subjected to ferocious scrutiny by General Burgoyne and others — is presented by Gleig as an act of political vindictiveness against a man whose principal crime was to have succeeded brilliantly. Modern historians have taken a considerably dimmer view.

The Dictionary of National Biography records that Gleig also wrote biographies of Warren Hastings and Sir Thomas Munro, making him the leading Victorian chronicler of the men who built the Company's empire. Macaulay, who had written a famous essay on Clive for the Edinburgh Review, was withering about Gleig's biography of Hastings — 'three big, bad volumes, full of undigested correspondence and undiscerning panegyric' — a judgement that reflects as much on Macaulay's vanity as on Gleig's limitations. The Life of Clive is a more controlled and readable performance.

To read Gleig's Life of Clive in 1858 — the year following the Indian Mutiny — is to read it in an atmosphere of heightened imperial anxiety and renewed debate about the nature of British rule in India. The Mutiny had resulted in the formal dissolution of the East India Company and the transfer of India to the Crown. Gleig does not address these events directly, but the biography stands as a defence of the tradition of individual initiative and military enterprise that had built the empire — a tradition whose costs were becoming harder to ignore.
contents: Clive's early life in Shropshire and arrival in India as a Company clerk, 1743
The Carnatic Wars and the defence of Arcot, 1751: the making of a military reputation
The Battle of Plassey, 1757: the foundations of British Bengal
The Parliamentary inquiry of 1772–73: corruption charges and Clive's defence
Clive's death in 1774 and the legacy of his Bengal administration

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Sixth — Catalogue No. LXVI
books.index_title: Adam Bede
books.author: George Eliot
subtitle_lines: The Novels of George Eliot
edition_lines: A Volume of the Blackwood Collected Edition
books.imprint: Printed for William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London; undated [s.a.]
essay: Adam Bede (1859) was George Eliot's first full-length novel, and it made her, overnight, the most talked-about new novelist in Britain — before anyone knew who 'George Eliot' was. This copy comes from the uniform Novels of George Eliot issued over many years by Blackwood, her lifelong publisher; it is undated and honestly foxed, one of the durable library reprints that kept her within reach of ordinary readers long after the three-volume first edition had become a collector's item.

The novel is set in the rural Loamshire of 1799 and turns on a seduction and its consequences: Adam Bede, the upright village carpenter; his love for the pretty, vain, self-absorbed Hetty Sorrel; the idle young squire Arthur Donnithorne, who ruins her; and Dinah Morris, the Methodist woman preacher whose steadiness holds the moral centre of the book. Hetty's concealed pregnancy, her flight, the death of her child and her trial for infanticide give the novel a tragic weight that startled its first readers, who had not expected such things from a débutante.

What announced a major writer was less the plot than the quality of attention. Eliot brought to English rural life a seriousness and a sympathy it had rarely been given — insisting that the inner lives of farmers and carpenters and dairymaids were as worthy of a novelist's full moral intelligence as those of dukes. The book was a huge commercial success, and the mystery of its authorship (the pseudonym concealed Marian Evans, a formidable intellectual living unmarried with a married man) only sharpened the public appetite.

Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) had come to fiction late and by an unlikely road: a provincial Warwickshire upbringing, a loss of religious faith, years as a translator and as the effective editor of the Westminster Review, and an unconventional and devoted union with George Henry Lewes that scandalised respectable society. She began writing fiction at around thirty-seven, under a man's name, and became the greatest English novelist of ideas — the mind behind Middlemarch. Adam Bede is where that career begins.

The book sits well beside the 1885 Cabinet Edition volumes of Eliot already in this library: the same author in a different, humbler dress. The foxing is not a defect so much as a record — the mark of a cheap, well-made, much-handled reprint that did the real work of a great novel, which is to be read. It is uniform with the Silas Marner catalogued below, the two having arrived together.
contents: Rural Loamshire, 1799 — village life rendered with unprecedented seriousness
Adam Bede, carpenter; Hetty Sorrel; Arthur Donnithorne; Dinah Morris, preacher

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fourteenth — Catalogue No. XIV
books.index_title: Les Moines d'Occident depuis Saint Benoit jusqu'a Saint Bernard
books.author: Le Comte de Montalembert
subtitle_lines: depuis Saint Benoit jusqu'a Saint Bernard
edition_lines: Le Comte de Montalembert, Membre de l'Academie Francaise
books.imprint: Publié par J. Lecoffre et Compagnie — Paris, MDCCCLX
essay: Les Moines d'Occident is the great unfinished masterpiece of French Catholic Romanticism — a monumental history of Western monasticism from its origins in the Egyptian desert through the age of Bede, Boniface and Alcuin to the eve of Saint Bernard and the twelfth-century renaissance of Clairvaux. Montalembert published the first two volumes in 1860, intending to reach Saint Bernard; three further volumes followed on the monks in England; he died in 1870 before completing the work; and the sixth and seventh volumes were assembled posthumously from his manuscripts by his friend Foisset and his son-in-law the Vicomte de Meaux. He had planned the project as early as 1835 — a quarter century of research and meditation lie behind every page.

The argument of the work is at once historical and polemical. Montalembert believed that the monasteries of the early medieval West had been the sole preservers of civilisation during the catastrophe of the barbarian invasions — that without Benedict and his rule, Gregory the Great, Columba, and Bede, the accumulated learning of the ancient world would have perished entirely, and that the subsequent history of Europe, including the liberty and culture that Montalembert valued, would have been impossible. This is not a view that modern historians accept without qualification, but it is argued with a learning, passion, and rhetorical force that make it impossible simply to dismiss.

Charles-Forbes-René, Comte de Montalembert (1810–1870), was born in London of an Anglo-Scottish mother and a French father who had served in the army of Condé. He was educated in England and brought to France at the Restoration, and he spent his life as the most eloquent spokesman for a liberal Catholicism that sought to reconcile the Church with constitutional government, freedom of the press, and the rights of nationalities. He was a member of the French Academy, a peer of France under Louis-Philippe, and a member of the Legislative Assembly under the Second Republic. His increasingly strained relationship with the ultramontane party — which regarded his liberalism as a betrayal of Catholic unity — shadowed the last decade of his life.

The authorised English translation, made by Mrs. Margaret Oliphant and published by Blackwood in Edinburgh from 1861, gave the work an immediate readership in Britain. The English title — The Monks of the West, from St. Benedict to St. Bernard — was adopted and the French text translated with scholarly fidelity. This first volume in French, which the Connolly Library holds, is the original Paris edition: the text as Montalembert intended it, before the English version intervened with its translator's compromises and its different scholarly apparatus.

That Les Moines d'Occident should be here in its French original, in an Irish library, is not entirely surprising. Montalembert had a particular sympathy with Ireland — a Catholic nation under Protestant rule — and the Irish Catholic educated class of the mid-nineteenth century followed French Catholic intellectual life with close attention. The book belongs to that world: the world of Daniel O'Connell's generation, of the Catholic University, of an Ireland that looked to continental Catholicism for intellectual validation. It is a magnificent and slightly uncomfortable object — the kind of book that was absolutely certain of its own importance, and was largely right.
contents: Book I — The Roman Empire after the peace of the Church: the social and spiritual context of early monasticism
Book II — Monastic precursors in the East: the Desert Fathers and the origins of the ascetic tradition
Book III — Monastic precursors in the West: from Cassian to the founding of Monte Cassino
Book IV — Saint Benedict and his Rule: the foundation of Western monasticism
Book V — Saint Gregory the Great: the Benedictine pope who sent Augustine to England

books.index_title: Silas Marner
books.author: George Eliot
subtitle_lines: The Weaver of Raveloe
The Novels of George Eliot
edition_lines: Uniform with Adam Bede in the Blackwood Collected Edition
books.imprint: Printed for William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London; undated [s.a.]
essay: Silas Marner (1861) is the shortest, and in construction the most perfect, of George Eliot's novels — a moral fable told with the economy of a folk tale and the psychological truth of a great realist. This is the Blackwood Novels of George Eliot reprint, undated and foxed, Volume III of the set, uniform with the Adam Bede catalogued above; the two came into this library together, a matched pair rescued from the same shelf.

The story is well known and perfectly shaped. Silas Marner, a linen-weaver wrongly cast out of his chapel community, exiles himself to the village of Raveloe and shrinks into a miser, living for the hoard of gold he counts each night. The gold is stolen; and into the void it leaves there wanders, one snowy evening, a golden-haired orphan child, Eppie, whom he takes in and raises. The exchange — dead metal for a living child — is the whole moral engine of the book, and Eliot makes of it something neither sentimental nor slight.

The novel has often been condescended to, partly because its length and clarity made it a fixture of the school syllabus, and a book set for examinations is easily mistaken for a simple one. It is not simple. Beneath the fairy-tale surface is a precise study of loss, isolation, and the slow re-knitting of a human being into a community — and, in the subplot of the Cass brothers, a hard look at the moral cost of respectability bought with a concealed truth.

Its author, Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880), wrote it quickly, between the larger labours of The Mill on the Floss and Romola, almost as a relief — and produced, without apparent strain, the most flawless thing she ever made. It has the quality of a story that has always existed, which is the rarest achievement in fiction and the hardest to plan.

This copy is a second Silas Marner for the library, standing beside the 1885 Cabinet Edition volume already here (Cat. XXVII). The foxing is honourable age; the plain Blackwood binding is the everyday dress in which most Victorians actually met the book. With its uniform Adam Bede it makes a small, pleasing island of matched volumes among the collection.

The stolen hoard of gold and the foundling child, Eppie
A moral fable of loss, isolation and restoration

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifteenth — Catalogue No. XV
books.index_title: All the Year Round — A Weekly Journal, Volume XI
books.author: Conducted by Charles Dickens
subtitle_lines: A Weekly Journal — Volume the Eleventh (February 13 to August 6, 1864)
books.imprint: Published at the Office of All the Year Round, 26 Wellington Street, Strand, London — and at Chapman and Hall, Piccadilly — MDCCCLXIV
essay: All the Year Round was Dickens's second great editorial venture and his most personal — a weekly journal that he founded in 1859, owned outright, and controlled absolutely, having quarrelled with his previous publishers Bradbury and Evans over their refusal to print his statement on his separation from his wife in their other publication, Punch. The journal superseded Household Words and carried above its masthead a quotation from Othello: 'The story of my life from year to year.' Volume XI, running from February to August 1864, appeared at the height of Dickens's editorial powers and in the year that saw him begin work on Our Mutual Friend — the last novel he would complete before his death in 1870.

The journal combined serial fiction and non-fiction articles in a format that Dickens had refined over decades of periodical journalism: double-columned, twenty-four pages, priced at twopence, unillustrated, appearing every Saturday. The fiction was always given the first position; the non-fiction covered international affairs, science, travel, social commentary, and whatever caught the interest of Dickens and his staff. Volume XI would have contained instalments of novels running through the spring and summer of 1864 — likely including George Sala's Quite Alone, which serialised through that period — along with the characteristic mixture of reportage and reflection.

Dickens's editorial policy for the non-fiction was deliberate and idiosyncratic. He instructed his staff to avoid the American Civil War as a topic unless a subject had been specifically cleared with him first — a policy reflecting his anxiety about alienating either American readership or British opinion. Nearly eleven percent of the non-fiction articles dealt with international affairs or foreign cultures; the journal was notably less interested in the domestic social journalism that had characterised Household Words, and considerably more interested in literary matters and in the international dimensions of Victorian life.

Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was, by 1864, the most famous living writer in the English language. He had published David Copperfield, Bleak House, Hard Times, Little Dorrit, A Tale of Two Cities, and Great Expectations; he had separated from his wife Catherine after twenty-two years of marriage; he had fallen in love with the young actress Ellen Ternan; and he was conducting a punishing schedule of public readings that would ultimately contribute to his death. The journal he conducted was, among other things, a financial anchor — a reliable income that gave him the independence to write his later novels at the pace they required.

A full run of All the Year Round in its original weekly numbers or in the annual bound volumes is one of the more substantial monuments to Victorian literary culture. The journal ran from 1859 to 1895, long outlasting Dickens himself under the editorship of his son Charles Jr. Volume XI is a single link in that long chain — twenty-six weeks of weekly publication, twenty-four pages each, bound together as a volume for those subscribers who wished to preserve them. To open it is to open a window into the middle of a particular week in the spring or summer of 1864, when a reader in London bought their Saturday copy and sat down, for tuppence, to read what Dickens had chosen for them.
contents: Serial fiction: novels running through February to August 1864, including George Sala's Quite Alone
International affairs and foreign correspondence: Dickens's particular interest in European and global events
Science, travel, and social commentary: the non-fiction staple of the journal
Dickens's editorial voice: the selection of topics, the house style, and the journal's distinctive tone
The Christmas number for 1864 (Mrs. Lirriper's Legacy): a separate collaborative venture with Collins, Edwards and others

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixteenth — Catalogue No. XVI
books.index_title: Our Mutual Friend
books.author: Charles Dickens
subtitle_lines: In Two Volumes
books.imprint: Published by Chapman and Hall, 193 Piccadilly — London, MDCCCLXV. With Forty Illustrations by Marcus Stone
essay: Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last completed novel and, by the reckoning of most serious readers, one of his greatest. It was published in twenty monthly parts between May 1864 and November 1865, at one shilling each, the final double number costing two. The bound two-volume edition appeared from Chapman and Hall in 1865, with forty wood-engraved illustrations by Marcus Stone, the son of a former neighbour and close friend of Dickens who had died the previous year. Stone's illustrations are quieter and more melancholy than Phiz's work on the earlier novels — fitting for a book that is itself darker, stranger, and more deliberately structured than anything Dickens had previously attempted.

The novel circles obsessively around money and its corruptions — around the Harmon dust heap, that great mound of Victorian refuse from which a fortune has been made, and around the Thames, which receives the city's dead and occasionally returns them. John Harmon, presumed drowned, lives under a false name among those who will inherit his father's fortune. The Veneerings give dinners for people they barely know. Mr. Boffin, the Golden Dustman, appears to be ruined by wealth. Lizzie Hexam, daughter of a Thames scavenger, is the moral centre of a novel that otherwise has few. The plot is intricate, at times almost wilfully so, and Dickens knew it: he built up a safety net of five completed numbers before Part I appeared in May 1864.

The composition was not easy. 'I have dropped astern this month instead of going ahead,' he reported in August 1864. In June 1865, returning from a holiday in France with Ellen Ternan, Dickens was involved in the Staplehurst rail disaster, in which ten passengers died. He spent hours among the injured and dying before retrieving from the wreck the manuscript of the number he had been carrying. The trauma, from which he never fully recovered, is acknowledged in the novel's Postscript with characteristic understatement. He came two and a half pages short for the following number.

Henry James, reviewing the novel in 1865, pronounced it Dickens's worst — an assessment that tells us more about James at twenty-two than about the novel. The twentieth century reversed this verdict almost completely. Edmund Wilson's essay 'Dickens: The Two Scrooges' (1941) identified Our Mutual Friend as the work in which Dickens most fully confronted the darkness of Victorian society; since then its reputation has risen steadily. It is now regarded as one of the most formally sophisticated novels in the language — a book about resurrection, about the redemption possible through assuming a false identity, about what money does to the people who want it and the people who have it.

Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was fifty-two when he began publishing Our Mutual Friend and fifty-three when it concluded. He had six years left. He would begin one more novel — The Mystery of Edwin Drood — and leave it unfinished at his death at Gad's Hill Place on 9 June 1870. Our Mutual Friend is the place to see what he might have done with those six years: a Dickens who had moved beyond comedy and melodrama into something harder to categorise, something closer to the late Shakespeare — last plays, complex, deliberately difficult, full of forgiveness and death.
contents: Book the First — The Cup and the Lip: the Harmon dust heap, the Thames, and the presumed death of John Harmon
Book the Second — Birds of a Feather: the Veneering dinners; Lizzie Hexam and Eugene Wrayburn
Book the Third — A Long Lane: Bella Wilfer and the Boffins; the school and Bradley Headstone
Book the Fourth — A Sunny Spot: resolution, resurrection, and the return of John Harmon
Forty illustrations by Marcus Stone; Postscript alluding to the Staplehurst rail disaster of June 1865

books.eyebrow: Entry the Seventeenth — Catalogue No. XVII
books.index_title: The Technical Educator — An Encyclopaedia of Technical Education, Vols. I & II
books.author: Cassell, Petter, Galpin & Co.
subtitle_lines: An Encyclopaedia of Technical Education — Volumes I & II
edition_lines: Published by Cassell, Petter, Galpin & Co.
books.imprint: London, Paris & New York: Cassell, Petter, Galpin & Co. — c.MDCCCLXXII. With Chromolithograph Frontispieces and Numerous Engravings
essay: The Technical Educator was Cassell's follow-up to their enormously successful Popular Educator (1852–55), applying the same principles of cheap, accessible self-instruction to the applied sciences and practical trades. Where the Popular Educator had covered languages, elementary mathematics, history, and general knowledge, the Technical Educator turned to civil engineering, mining and quarrying, photography, mechanical drawing, applied chemistry, architecture, and the design of manufactured objects. Published in four volumes (this library holding Volumes I and II), it appeared around 1870–72, undated as issued — a common practice of Cassell's — and was printed in the large octavo format that made it a substantial and handsome reference.

The house of Cassell was itself a remarkable institution. John Cassell (1817–1865) was born in Manchester, the son of a public-house landlord, apprenticed to a joiner, and self-educated. He came to London in 1836, threw his energies into the temperance movement, established himself as a tea and coffee merchant in 1847, and almost simultaneously began publishing cheap literature for the working classes. His firm, which became Cassell, Petter, Galpin & Co. in 1859, produced the Popular Educator, the Technical Educator, the Magazine of Art, and editions of standard works at prices the working man could afford. It was an act of idealism made commercially viable — the belief that self-improvement was possible, and that cheap print could enable it.

Among the contributors to the Technical Educator was Christopher Dresser (1834–1904), whose essays on decorative design later appeared in expanded form in his Principles of Decorative Design (1873), one of the foundational texts of the Victorian design reform movement. Dresser was the first industrial designer in the modern sense — a man who applied the principles of botany and art to the design of manufactured objects, and who argued that beauty and utility were not merely compatible but inseparable. His presence in the Technical Educator's pages places this practical reference work at the edge of a larger aesthetic argument about what Victorian industry was for.

The volumes are illustrated throughout with black-and-white engravings showing technical processes, machinery, and architectural details, each volume preceded by a chromolithograph frontispiece — the period's most vivid and expensive colour printing technology. The sections on mining and quarrying, steam engines, and civil engineering reflect the enormous infrastructure projects of the mid-Victorian decades: the railway network, the sewers, the bridges, the harbours. The book is in this sense a documentary record of the physical world being built around its readers.

The Technical Educator belongs to a Victorian genre that no longer quite exists: the encyclopaedia addressed to the intelligent adult who wished to understand, and perhaps to enter, the technical world being created around them. Its readership was men who had left school at twelve and wished to know how a suspension bridge was calculated, how a photograph was developed, how iron was smelted. That these men existed in sufficient numbers to make such a publication commercially viable is itself a historical fact of some consequence.
contents: Civil engineering: bridges, railways, canals, harbours — the infrastructure of Victorian Britain
Mining and quarrying: methods, machinery, and mineral products
Photography: the chemistry and practical technique of the new art
Mechanical drawing and applied geometry: the draughtsman's craft
Essays on decorative design by Christopher Dresser — later expanded into Principles of Decorative Design (1873)

books.eyebrow: Entry the Eighteenth — Catalogue No. XVIII
books.index_title: Memoires de Turenne — Precis des Guerres du Marechal de Turenne
books.author: Napoleon Bonaparte (dictated at St. Helena)
subtitle_lines: Precis des Guerres du Marechal de Turenne — dicte par Napoleon a Sainte-Helene
books.imprint: Publie par Hachette et Compagnie — Paris, MDCCCLXXII
essay: This is Napoleon's own military commentary on the campaigns of Henri de la Tour d'Auvergne, Vicomte de Turenne (1611–1675) — France's greatest marshal before Napoleon himself. It was dictated at Longwood House on St Helena, not to Turenne's memory alone but as part of Napoleon's vast autobiographical project: the systematic construction, in captivity, of the legend by which he wished to be remembered. He dictated the Precis des guerres du marechal Turenne to General Gourgaud, one of the small company of soldiers and courtiers who had chosen exile with him on that remote Atlantic island, and it was published as part of the Memoires pour servir a l'histoire de France series first issued between 1823 and 1825. This Hachette edition of 1872 is one of the many reprints that kept the text in circulation throughout the nineteenth century.

Turenne was Napoleon's ideal of a commander: patient, methodical, capable of strategic retreat without loss of nerve, and — unlike Napoleon himself — never destroyed by overreach. Napoleon's commentary on his campaigns in Alsace, the Rhineland, and the Low Countries is both a work of military analysis and a form of self-portraiture by contrast and identification. In annotating Turenne, Napoleon was defining what he believed a great commander to be — and implicitly defending his own record against the verdict of Waterloo.
