Ten days before his death in May 1821, he ordered his Grand Marshal Bertrand to publish his campaigns in Italy and Egypt for his son, adding that 'Caesar, Turenne and Frederick were of little worth' — a gesture of supreme arrogance or supreme despair, or both.

The circumstances of composition could hardly be more extraordinary. Napoleon at Longwood was a man with nothing left but time and memory. The house was damp, the climate oppressive, the English governor Hudson Lowe hostile and suspicious. Las Cases, Montholon, Gourgaud, and Bertrand took turns as his secretaries, transcribing his dictations, which he then corrected in his own hand. He moved between campaigns as the mood took him — the Italian war to Gourgaud one afternoon, the Egyptian expedition to Montholon the next morning. The Turenne commentary was one of the works he considered most nearly finished at his death.

Henri de Turenne himself had been the dominant French commander of Louis XIV's early wars, conducting the campaigns in Alsace and the Rhine valley that secured France's eastern frontier. He died in 1675 at Sassbach, killed by a cannon ball while observing the enemy lines — a death Napoleon noted with the admiration of a fellow professional. Turenne's strategic flexibility, his ability to operate on interior lines and to use space as a military resource, provided Napoleon with models he had applied in his own Italian campaigns of 1796–97 and that he analysed here with the clarity of a mind still, in captivity, fiercely alive.

Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821) was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, a year after France acquired the island from Genoa. He was educated at military school in Brienne and Paris, served as an artillery officer in the revolutionary armies, rose through genius and ambition to become First Consul in 1799 and Emperor in 1804, dominated Europe for a decade, and was finally overthrown in 1815. He died at Longwood House on 5 May 1821, almost certainly of stomach cancer, aged fifty-one. The Precis des guerres du marechal Turenne is one of the last substantial works he completed — a soldier's meditation on a soldier, written on a rock in the Atlantic.
contents: The campaigns in Alsace, 1674–75: Turenne's masterly recovery after the fall of Breisach
The Rhineland operations: interior lines, strategic withdrawal, and the relief of Alsace
Napoleon's general analysis of Turenne's method: patience, manoeuvre, and the use of ground
Comparative notes on Turenne's campaigns and Napoleon's own Italian operations of 1796–97
Appendix: Precis des campagnes and additional manuscript notes corrected by Napoleon's own hand

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Seventh — Catalogue No. LXVII
books.index_title: Romola
books.author: George Eliot
subtitle_lines: A Romance of Renaissance Florence
edition_lines: Author of Adam Bede and Middlemarch
books.imprint: Printed for Smith, Elder and Co. — London, MDCCCLXXIII
essay: Romola is the great historical novel of George Eliot's middle years — the book she said had aged her more than any other. 'I began it a young woman,' she remarked, 'and I finished it an old woman.' It was serialised, with illustrations by Frederic Leighton, in the Cornhill Magazine across 1862–63; this is the Smith, Elder reprint of October 1873, one of the steady stream of printings that kept the novel before the Victorian public. It is a distinct edition from the 1885 Cabinet Romola already catalogued in this library (Cat. XXV) — the same novel in an earlier London dress.

The setting is Florence at the end of the fifteenth century, in the convulsive years of Lorenzo de' Medici's death, the French invasion, and the rise and burning of the friar Savonarola. At its centre are Tito Melema — charming, clever, and morally weightless, a study in the small betrayals by which a man loses his soul — and Romola de' Bardi, the blind scholar's daughter whose slow moral awakening gives the book its title and its conscience.

It is the most laboured of Eliot's novels and, for some readers, the most heavy-going: the Florentine learning sits close to the surface, and the historical apparatus can weigh on the story. But it is also her most ambitious bid for European stature — a deliberate move beyond the English rural world of Adam Bede toward the grand canvas of Renaissance humanism. George Smith paid her £7,000 for it, the largest sum yet offered an English novelist, a measure of what her name had become.

The novel repays the patient reader with one of Eliot's finest moral portraits. Tito's ruin is achieved not by any single great crime but by a chain of comfortable evasions, each reasonable in the moment; it is among the most exact anatomies in fiction of how an agreeable man becomes a treacherous one. Romola's answering movement — from private devotion toward a hard-won, disillusioned goodness — is the counterweight the book is built around.

To own a novel in more than one edition is a particular and slightly indefensible pleasure, and this Romola is here for exactly that reason: an earlier, plainer, London printing to sit alongside the Cabinet copy. Together they show a book at different points in its long life — the same Florence, the same Savonarola, in two different bindings on the same shelves.
contents: Renaissance Florence in the age of Savonarola, 1490s
Tito Melema — the anatomy of a man's moral drift
Romola de' Bardi — a slow awakening to conscience
Serialised in the Cornhill (1862–63) with Leighton's illustrations
Smith, Elder & Co. reprint, London 1873; distinct from the 1885 Cabinet copy (Cat. XXV)

books.eyebrow: Entry the Nineteenth — Catalogue No. XIX
books.index_title: Leila; or, The Siege of Granada
books.author: Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton
title_lines: Leila; or, The Siege of Granada
subtitle_lines: Together with Calderon the Courtier
edition_lines: Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton, Bart., M.P., Author of 'The Last Days of Pompeii', &c.
books.imprint: Published by George Routledge and Sons — London, MDCCCLXXV
essay: Leila; or, The Siege of Granada was first published in 1838, at the height of Bulwer-Lytton's early fame, and belongs to the same vein of high historical romance as his more celebrated The Last Days of Pompeii (1834). It is set in Granada in the summer and autumn of 1491, as Ferdinand and Isabella's Christian forces tighten their siege of the last Moorish kingdom in Spain. Against this backdrop of collision between three civilisations — Christian, Moorish, and Jewish — Bulwer-Lytton weaves a story of impossible loyalties and inevitable tragedy, its central figure the Jewish scholar Almamen, whose shifting allegiances between the Moorish Boabdil and the Christian besiegers destroy everyone he loves including his daughter Leila.

The novel's three-way religious drama is its most distinctive feature. Almamen is a Kabbalist and an Israelite patriot who dreams of using the conflict between Moor and Christian to restore Jewish independence in Spain — a fantasy that the novel treats with both sympathy and the inevitability of doom. His daughter Leila, captured by the Christians and under pressure to convert, is caught between her father's world and a love for a Spanish knight. The historical backdrop — the fall of Granada on 2 January 1492, and the expulsion of the Jews from Spain that followed — gives these personal tragedies their weight. It is a novel acutely aware that history moves through and over individuals without regard for their sufferings.

Edward Bulwer-Lytton (1803–1873) was one of the most professionally successful writers of the Victorian period and one of the most critically abused. He wrote in almost every genre: the fashionable silver-fork novel, the historical romance, the Newgate crime fiction, the domestic comedy, the occult tale, the utopian fantasy. He coined the phrase 'the great unwashed,' popularised the opening 'It was a dark and stormy night,' and was satirised by Thackeray as 'Sir Lytton Doddery.' He was also a Member of Parliament for many years and served briefly as Colonial Secretary. His first wife Rosina Wheeler waged a public campaign of denunciation against him for decades, including an appearance at one of his political hustings.

This 1875 edition from Routledge is a later reprint of a novel that had been in print for nearly forty years by this date — a measure of Bulwer-Lytton's sustained popularity across the Victorian period. The bound volume also contains Calderon the Courtier, a shorter historical tale set at the court of Philip II of Spain, which had originally appeared as a companion piece to Leila. The two together form a sustained engagement with Spanish history at its most dramatic — the moment when the medieval world of three religions in uneasy coexistence was swept away by the violent assertion of Catholic unity.

Leila was written in the same year as Dickens's Oliver Twist and Carlyle's French Revolution — a vintage year for English prose. It is a lesser work than either, but it is not negligible. Its treatment of the Jewish predicament in 1491 has a dignity that the novel's more theatrical episodes sometimes undermine; and the final fall of Granada, observed from inside the vanishing world rather than from the triumphant outside, is genuinely affecting. The 1875 reader who opened this Routledge edition was opening a book that had been consistently in print for the whole of Victoria's reign.
contents: Part I — Granada in 1491: the Moorish court of Boabdil and the gathering Christian siege
Part II — Almamen the Kabbalist: the Jewish scholar's impossible dream of national restoration
Part III — Leila between worlds: conversion, love, and the failure of refuge
The fall of Granada, January 1492 — and the expulsion of the Jews that followed
Calderon the Courtier: a companion tale of love and honour at the court of Philip II

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twentieth — Catalogue No. XX
books.index_title: The Dramatic Works of William Shakespeare — Volume II
books.author: William Shakespeare
title_lines: The Dramatic Works of William Shakespeare
subtitle_lines: Volume the Second
books.imprint: Published 1875
essay: To catalogue a volume of Shakespeare is to catalogue a library within a library — for no author has been more variously edited, more frequently reprinted, more differently presented to successive reading publics than the man from Stratford. The 1875 date places this volume in the great Victorian Shakespeare moment: the period bracketed by the Cambridge Shakespeare of Clark and Wright (1863–66), which established the standard scholarly text, and the flood of popular editions that followed — Routledge, Ward & Lock, Cassell, Chambers — each seeking to place the plays in the hands of a reading public that had been told, by a century of Romantic criticism, that Shakespeare was the supreme expression of the human spirit.

Volume II of a collected dramatic works, whatever the edition, typically contains the middle comedies and histories — the plays of Shakespeare's mature early period: As You Like It, Much Ado About Nothing, The Merry Wives of Windsor, perhaps Twelfth Night or The Merchant of Venice, and the great English history cycle of the Henry IVs, Henry V, and their companions. These are the plays in which Shakespeare's range first becomes fully apparent: the capacity to move from the philosophical comedy of Rosalind and Touchstone to the political realism of Falstaff and Prince Hal without any apparent strain.

The Victorian Shakespeare was above all a schoolroom and a drawing-room Shakespeare — a text for domestic reading, for recitation, for the improvement of the young. The great popular editions were typically introduced with biographical and critical prefaces that situated the plays within a narrative of genius: the Stratford boyhood, the London theatre, the retirement to New Place. Illustration was common, ranging from wood-engraved vignettes to chromolithographic frontispieces reproducing scenes from celebrated paintings or theatrical productions. The binding was designed to sit well on a shelf, to look like culture.

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, the son of a glover and alderman. He was educated at the local grammar school, married Anne Hathaway at eighteen, had three children, and by the early 1590s was established in London as an actor and playwright. Between approximately 1590 and 1613 he wrote the thirty-seven plays and one hundred and fifty-four sonnets that constitute the largest single body of literary work in the English language. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there in 1616. His plays were first collected in the First Folio of 1623, assembled by his fellow actors Heminge and Condell. Every edition since is an act of interpretation.

To hold a Victorian Shakespeare is to hold a particular moment in the long relationship between these texts and their readers — a moment when the plays were being simultaneously elevated to a near-religious status by critics and made cheaply available to an unprecedentedly wide reading public. The tension between reverence and accessibility, between the scholarly apparatus of the critical edition and the plain text of the people's edition, runs through every Victorian Shakespeare. Whatever edition this is, it carries that tension in its binding, its typography, and its presence in this library.
contents: The middle comedies: As You Like It, Much Ado About Nothing, The Merry Wives of Windsor
The problem of the middle histories: the Henry IV plays and Henry V
Editorial apparatus: preface, biographical note, and textual commentary
Illustrations: wood-engraved vignettes or chromolithographic plates after contemporary paintings
The Victorian Shakespeare in context: popular editions and the democratisation of literary culture

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Second — Catalogue No. LXII
books.index_title: Many Thoughts of Many Minds
books.author: Henry Southgate
subtitle_lines: Selections from the Writings of the Most Celebrated Authors
from the Earliest to the Present Time
books.imprint: Printed for Charles Griffin and Company — London, MDCCCLXXVII
essay: Many Thoughts of Many Minds is one of the great monuments of Victorian self-improvement: an enormous commonplace book, gathering into a single volume several thousand passages of prose and verse drawn from the most celebrated authors 'from the earliest to the present time,' and arranged — as the title page proudly insists — analytically, by subject. It was first assembled by Henry Southgate in the late 1850s and published by Charles Griffin and Company; it proved so popular that it ran through edition after edition and spawned a second series, the whole becoming a fixture of the respectable Victorian drawing-room. The 1877 volume here is one stage in that long and prosperous life.

The book belongs to a tradition older than printing — the commonplace book, in which a reader copied out the passages worth keeping — but Southgate industrialised it. Where a private commonplace book recorded one mind's reading, Many Thoughts offered the reader the digested reading of an entire civilisation, sorted under headings so that a passage on Death, or Friendship, or Adversity, could be found at need. It is the close English cousin of Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, which had appeared in America in 1855, and it answered the same hunger: a rising, self-educating middle class that wished to have the wisdom of the ages within arm's reach, and ideally within quoting distance at dinner.

What the book preserves, almost despite itself, is a portrait of the Victorian mind — of what that age considered worth remembering. Shakespeare and the Bible tower over everything; Bacon, Milton, the English poets and the great divines crowd the pages; the tone is overwhelmingly moral, improving and earnest. To read it now is to be told, passage by passage, what a cultivated person in 1877 was expected to feel about the large subjects of life. It is a reference book, but it is also, read straight through, an unintended anthology of an entire sensibility.

Henry Southgate (1818–1888) was, by profession, exactly this: a compiler and anthologist, a maker of such volumes rather than an author in his own right. He produced several companions to this one — Noble Thoughts in Noble Language, Gone Before, Things a Lady would like to Know — all in the same improving spirit. His own contribution was arrangement and prefatory essay rather than original composition, and he is remembered, where he is remembered at all, for the labour of selection and ordering. It is honest work, and harder than it looks; the choices an anthologist makes are themselves a kind of authorship.

There is a particular pleasure in finding a book like this in a living library, because its whole purpose was to be used — opened at the relevant heading, quoted, returned to. It is the ancestor of every book of quotations, every desk reference, every search box into which one now types a half-remembered line. That a heavy Victorian volume of other men's words should still sit on a shelf, consulted or merely kept, is a quiet vindication of the thing Southgate believed: that the best of what has been thought and said is worth gathering up and keeping close.
contents: Several thousand selections arranged analytically by subject
Passages from Shakespeare, the Bible, Bacon and the English poets prominently represented
Prose and verse 'from the earliest to the present time'
The compiler's prefatory essays on reading and quotation
Published by Charles Griffin and Company, London

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-First — Catalogue No. XXI
books.index_title: The Swiss Family Robinson
books.author: J. R. Wyss; translated & edited by John Lovell
subtitle_lines: Translated and Edited from Stahl's 'Nouveau Robinson Suisse'
edition_lines: Johann David Wyss — Translated and Edited by John Lovell
books.imprint: Published by Cassell, Petter, Galpin & Co. — London, Paris & New York, c.MDCCCLXXX. With Chromolithograph Frontispiece and Numerous Wood-Engraved Illustrations
essay: The Swiss Family Robinson is one of the most successfully transplanted books in literary history — a German text of 1812 that passed through a French translation, several English versions, countless abridgments and expansions, and finally the hands of John Lovell working from P. J. Stahl's French Nouveau Robinson Suisse to produce the illustrated Cassell edition that circulated through the nurseries and schoolrooms of the Victorian English-speaking world. At each stage of transmission, the text changed: episodes were added, sermons reduced, the botany corrected, the geography made slightly less impossible. The Swiss pastor and his four sons who survive a shipwreck in the East Indies are simultaneously Wyss's original characters and the creation of every translator who has touched them since.

Johann David Wyss (1743–1818) was himself a Swiss pastor, and like his narrator he had four sons — for whom the novel was originally devised as an instructive entertainment, a Robinson Crusoe equipped with the full resources of natural history and practical science. The father of his story knows everything: how to salt meat, how to build a bridge, how to process rubber, how to tame an onager. The island provides, with improbable generosity, representatives of almost every useful plant and animal known to natural history, regardless of their actual geographical distribution. This cheerful impossibility is part of the novel's appeal: it is a world arranged for the convenience of pedagogy.

Johann Rudolf Wyss (1782–1830), the author's son, edited and published his father's manuscript, completing and extending it substantially before it appeared in Zurich in 1812. The younger Wyss was himself a writer and poet who composed the Swiss national anthem. It was he who shaped the narrative into publishable form and saw it through the press. The French version by Isabelle de Montolieu (1816) added further episodes, including the subplot of Jenny Montrose, the English girl discovered on the island in the novel's final section — a subplot that most English editions retained, having derived from Montolieu rather than Wyss directly.

John Lovell's translation for Cassell, Petter & Galpin is the version that most Victorian children would have encountered: generously illustrated, well produced, and priced for the gift-book market. The chromolithograph frontispiece and the numerous wood-engraved illustrations throughout placed the island, its animals, and its improbably competent family before the reader's eye with the vivid specificity that Victorian illustrated publishing had made its signature. Cassell's had previously published The Technical Educator and other educational works from the same premises; the Swiss Family Robinson was their contribution to the large and profitable market for improving children's literature.

The novel's deeper appeal, beneath its encyclopaedic surface, is a fantasy of total self-sufficiency — of a family that needs nothing from the corrupt and complicated world it has left behind, that can build its civilisation from first principles on a providential island. This fantasy was peculiarly potent for the Victorian middle class, whose anxieties about economic dependence, social precariousness, and the fragility of respectability were precisely what the Robinsons of Felsenheim had overcome. The book is, in this reading, not a children's story at all but a family romance about the possibility of beginning again.
contents: The shipwreck and first landing: the family's survival and initial exploration of the island
The building of Felsenheim: tree house, farm, and the gradual creation of a self-sufficient settlement
Natural history as narrative: the island's flora and fauna as occasions for instruction and adventure
The discovery of Jenny Montrose (from Montolieu's additions): the English girl and the prospect of rescue
Illustrations: chromolithograph frontispiece and wood-engraved plates after drawings in the Cassell tradition

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Second — Catalogue No. XXII
books.index_title: Kingsthorpiana; or, Researches in a Church Chest
books.author: Rev. J. Hulbert Glover
subtitle_lines: or, Researches in a Church Chest — Being a Calendar of Old Documents now existing in the Church Chest of Kingsthorpe, near Northampton, with a Selection of the MSS. printed in full, and Extracts from others
edition_lines: Edited by the Rev. J. Hulbert Glover, M.A., Vicar of Kingsthorpe
books.imprint: Printed for Private Distribution — Northampton, MDCCCLXXXIII
essay: Kingsthorpiana is that most characteristic of Victorian antiquarian productions: the parish chest book. It was published privately in 1883 by the Reverend John Hulbert Glover, vicar of Kingsthorpe — the ancient village two miles north of Northampton that had been a separate parish only since 1850, its Norman church of St John the Baptist overlooking a village green that was already being swallowed by the expanding shoe-trade town beneath it. Glover had opened the church chest — the old oak box in which successive generations of churchwardens had deposited their documents, their accounts, their vestry minutes, their indentures, and their correspondence — and found, as anyone who opens such chests in English parish churches finds, a small buried world.

The documents calendared and transcribed here span centuries of parish life: churchwardens' accounts recording the purchase of wine and the repair of the steeple; vestry minutes settling disputes about pew rights and the schoolmaster's salary; indentures apprenticing poor boys of the parish to tradesmen in Northampton; receipts for the repair of the church bells. The earliest documents reach back to the medieval period; the latest are near-contemporary. Taken together they form an irreplaceable record of how a particular English community organised itself, taxed itself, buried its dead, educated its children, and argued about its boundaries — across the whole span of English Protestant history.

The Rev. John Hulbert Glover was evidently a man of the old clerical antiquarian type: a parish priest who found in local history a scholarly vocation that gave his ministry a second dimension. He would later, by deed poll dated 14 November 1900, establish the Glover Augmentation Fund for the parish — a personal endowment producing twenty-five pounds per annum in perpetuity for the augmentation of annuities payable under the Kingsthorpe Bounty, the old charitable fund for the parish poor. It is the act of a man who had spent his career thinking about his parish's past and its future simultaneously.

Kingsthorpe itself is a place of some historical density. Listed in Domesday as Torp, a Crown demesne, its name derives from the Old English cyning and Old Danish torp — the King's hamlet. Its church retains late Anglo-Saxon or early Norman windows, the north and south aisles added around 1170–80, the chancel rebuilt in the 1850s when the village was raised to full parochial status. The quarry on the parish's edge provided the white freestone used in the construction of the Northampton barracks, the General Hospital, and buildings in Sheep Street. The village was, in 1883, on the edge of absorption into the growing industrial town — a process completed when most of the civil parish was added to the Northampton municipal borough in 1900.

Books like Kingsthorpiana are among the most historically valuable and least read productions of the Victorian press. They were printed in small numbers for limited distribution, were never reviewed in the national journals, and survive in collections precisely because nobody thought them worth discarding. They are the raw material of local history — sometimes poorly organised, always partial, frequently charming in their assumption that the record of a particular vestry meeting or a particular apprenticeship indenture matters because it is true. Glover evidently believed this. The fact that his book survives in this library, four thousand miles from the church chest it describes, is its own small historical curiosity.
contents: Churchwardens' accounts: wine, candles, bell-ropes, and the maintenance of the fabric of St John the Baptist
Vestry minutes: pew rights, the schoolmaster's salary, and the governance of the parish poor
Apprenticeship indentures: the Pritchard and Cooke charity funds and the education of poor children
Medieval and early modern documents: the hospital of St David founded 1200, and pre-Reformation parish records
Index of persons, properties, and subjects mentioned in the church chest documents

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Third — Catalogue No. XXIII
books.index_title: Daniel Deronda
books.author: George Eliot
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXV. Cabinet Edition
essay: Daniel Deronda was published in eight monthly parts between February and September 1876, the last novel George Eliot completed. It is her most ambitious work and her most divided — divided in its narrative between the English country house world of Gwendolen Harleth, one of the great psychological portraits in Victorian fiction, and the parallel story of Daniel Deronda's discovery of his Jewish identity and his commitment to the Zionist project. Contemporary readers and critics tended to find the Gwendolen half magnificent and the Deronda half wearying. Henry James, predictably, agreed. Posterity has been more inclined to see the two halves as inseparable — the critique of English upper-class purposelessness requiring the counter-example of a community with a millennial purpose.

Gwendolen Harleth is Eliot's most brilliantly realised egoist: beautiful, clever, accustomed to governing, and utterly unprepared for the discovery that the world will not arrange itself according to her preferences. Her marriage to the cold, sadistic Grandcourt is one of the most disturbing relationships in Victorian fiction — a contract entered in full knowledge of its terms and repented with full understanding of why repentance comes too late. Her moral education at the hands of Daniel Deronda, who watches, counsels, and refuses to rescue her, is the novel's central drama. It is conducted with a psychological precision and moral seriousness that few writers before or since have matched.

The Jewish question was not incidental to Eliot's purposes. She had been reading and thinking about Jewish history, culture, and identity for years before writing the novel, and her portrait of Mordecai — the visionary, dying scholar who becomes Deronda's spiritual father — draws on that reading with a depth and seriousness that was unusual in an age when literary Jews were mostly comic or villainous. The novel's commitment to Jewish national aspiration, written more than twenty years before Herzl's Der Judenstaat (1896), has led some scholars to see Eliot as a proto-Zionist, though her vision was cultural and ethical rather than political.

George Eliot (1819–1880) was born Mary Ann Evans in Warwickshire, the daughter of a land agent. She was exceptionally well educated for a woman of her time, reading widely in German, French, Latin, and Greek, and became the de facto editor of the Westminster Review from 1851. Her long relationship with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes, who was legally married to another woman and could not divorce her, placed Eliot outside respectable society. It also freed her from its conventions. Her first fiction appeared in 1856; by the time of Daniel Deronda she was, by common critical consent, the greatest living English novelist.

The 1885 Cabinet Edition of George Eliot's Works, published by William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, represents the standard collected text of her fiction — the edition that readers throughout the late Victorian period would have used. It was supplemented in the same year by the three-volume biography, George Eliot's Life as Related in her Letters and Journals, arranged and edited by her husband John Walter Cross, who had married her in May 1880, seven months before her death in December of that year. The Cross biography was well-intentioned and deeply misleading, presenting a sanitised Eliot that bore little relation to the formidably independent woman her friends had known. It took decades of subsequent scholarship to recover the real one.
contents: Book I–II — Miss Harleth: Gwendolen's world, her losses at roulette, and the first encounter with Deronda
Book III–IV — Maidens Choosing: the Lapidoth family, Mirah, and the world of Jewish London
Book V–VI — Mordecai: the dying visionary, his dream of Jewish nationhood, and Deronda's response
Book VII–VIII — The Mother and the Son: Deronda's origins revealed; Gwendolen's crisis and partial redemption
The question of purposiveness: English society's emptiness set against Jewish historical consciousness

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Fourth — Catalogue No. XXIV
books.index_title: Middlemarch — A Study of Provincial Life
books.author: George Eliot
subtitle_lines: A Study of Provincial Life
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXV. Cabinet Edition
essay: Middlemarch was published in eight bi-monthly parts between December 1871 and December 1872, and is by general critical consent the greatest English novel. Virginia Woolf called it 'one of the few English novels written for grown-up people.' In 2015, writers from outside Britain voted it first among all British novels 'by a landslide.' Harold Bloom placed Eliot among the most important Western writers of all time, and Middlemarch was his primary evidence. Its opening declaration — that the history of Dorothea Brooke is 'one of those unhistoric acts' upon which rests 'the growing good of the world' — is as bold and as earned a statement as any in the literature.

The novel weaves four principal plots around the provincial town of Middlemarch in the English Midlands during the years 1829–32 — the years immediately preceding the Reform Act. Dorothea Brooke marries the aged scholar Casaubon in a catastrophic act of idealism, seeking a greatness she cannot find elsewhere; Tertius Lydgate comes to Middlemarch with medical ambitions and is destroyed by his marriage to Rosamond Vincy; Fred Vincy's debts and his love for Mary Garth constitute the novel's comic subplot; and Nicholas Bulstrode, the Evangelical banker, is finally exposed by the past he has suppressed. These four plots interact with extraordinary structural complexity and thematic coherence — Eliot managing a larger canvas of characters and relationships than any previous English novelist had attempted.

What holds the novel together is its narrator — the most intellectually engaged, morally serious, and sympathetically ironic narrative voice in the language. The narrator of Middlemarch knows more than any single character, but does not hold that knowledge over them; instead it uses its perspective to enlarge our understanding of each character's subjective world, making us simultaneously aware of their limitations and alive to their dignity. The famous passage on the 'roar on the other side of silence' — the suffering of those who ordinarily have no spokesman — is the novel's moral and aesthetic programme compressed into a sentence.

Middlemarch was Eliot's breakthrough to the largest possible canvas. It had been preceded by Adam Bede (1859), The Mill on the Floss (1860), Silas Marner (1861), Romola (1863), and Felix Holt (1866) — a sequence of novels each of which extended her range of time, place, and psychological ambition. But Middlemarch is the work in which all of those extensions are fully integrated. The provincial setting is both particular enough to be real and universal enough to contain the whole of English social life. The historical moment is chosen with precision: the novel is set just before the Reform Act not because Eliot wished to write about electoral reform but because the moment of political change reveals what people are made of.

This 1885 Blackwood Cabinet Edition brings together the text Eliot regarded as definitive. The Cabinet Edition of 1878, produced two years before her death, had been the first collected edition of her works, and it remained the standard scholarly text. The 1885 printing is one of several subsequent impressions from the same setting of type, produced by Blackwood to meet the sustained demand of a reading public that continued to treat George Eliot's novels as essential intellectual and moral equipment.
contents: Book I — Miss Brooke: Dorothea's idealism and her disastrous engagement to the antiquarian Casaubon
Book II — Old and Young: Lydgate's arrival; Rosamond Vincy and the web of provincial society
Book III — Waiting for Death: Casaubon's illness and the codicil; Fred Vincy's debts
Book IV–VIII — Three Love Problems, The Dead Hand, The Widow and the Wife, Two Temptations, Sunset and Sunrise
The Reform Act background; Bulstrode's fall; and Dorothea's 'unhistoric acts'

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Fifth — Catalogue No. XXV
books.index_title: Romola
books.author: George Eliot
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXV. Cabinet Edition
essay: Romola is the most extraordinary act of scholarly labour in Victorian fiction. It is set in Florence between 1492 and 1498 — the years of Lorenzo de' Medici's death, the French invasion under Charles VIII, the brief theocratic republic of Savonarola, and the beginning of the Italian crisis that would reshape European history. George Eliot spent years in preparation: learning Italian, reading Florentine history, studying the political and cultural life of the Republic, and making two extended visits to Florence. She told her publisher John Blackwood that she began the novel as one person and finished it as another — that the effort of historical imagination had transformed her.

The novel centres on Romola de' Bardi, daughter of a blind Florentine scholar, whose marriage to the Greek opportunist Tito Melema becomes a moral catastrophe as she watches the man she chose for his beauty and apparent brilliance reveal himself as a systematic betrayer of everyone who trusted him. Tito's progressive corruption is one of the most analytically precise studies of moral deterioration in Victorian fiction — Eliot tracking the small accommodations, the rationalised self-deceits, the incremental surrenders of principle that turn a gifted man into a destroyer. Against him stands Savonarola — the great Friar, burning reformer, prophet and fanatic — whose grip on Romola's conscience and whose ultimate failure constitute the novel's most challenging subplot.

Romola was serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from July 1862 to August 1863, illustrated by Frederic Leighton — one of the most ambitious visual collaborations in Victorian periodical history. George Smith, the Cornhill's proprietor, paid Eliot seven thousand pounds for it, then the highest price ever paid for a novel. Sales disappointed him: the historical setting, the Italian milieu, and the moral density of the narrative were too demanding for the general reader. The novel has never been truly popular. It has, however, been consistently admired by those who have read it carefully — Henry James among them, who called it Eliot's 'finest production.'

The historical reconstruction is remarkable not only for its accuracy but for its imaginative inhabitation of another century's values and assumptions. Eliot understood that fifteenth-century Florentines did not think as Victorians thought — that their categories of religious experience, political obligation, and personal honour were genuinely different from those of her own age. She attempted, with considerable success, to write a novel that was historically true in this deeper sense: not merely accurate in its costumes and architecture, but faithful to a way of being in the world that Victorian England had left behind.

Mary Ann Evans (George Eliot, 1819–1880) found Romola the most exhausting of her creative efforts. It cost her, she said, more blood than anything else she wrote — the blood of sustained historical imagination under the pressure of a monthly serial schedule. Her relationship with the novel was always ambivalent: she knew it was a great achievement and suspected it was not quite a success. The 1885 Cabinet Edition text represents her final thoughts on it, incorporating the revisions she made for the 1878 collected edition — the last time she would have read it through.
contents: Book I — The Visible Past: Florence 1492, the court of Lorenzo, and the arrival of Tito Melema
Book II — The Visible Past (continued): Romola's marriage and the beginning of Tito's betrayals
Book III — The Unseen Good: Savonarola's republic; Romola's crisis of faith and duty
The historical context: Lorenzo de' Medici, Charles VIII, Savonarola's bonfire of the vanities
Frederic Leighton's illustrations for the Cornhill Magazine serialisation, 1862–63

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Sixth — Catalogue No. XXVI
books.index_title: Felix Holt, the Radical
books.author: George Eliot
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXV. Cabinet Edition
essay: Felix Holt, the Radical was published in June 1866, set in the months surrounding the Reform Act of 1832, and represents Eliot's most sustained engagement with English political life. The title is something of a paradox: Felix Holt is a radical who believes that working-class men are not yet ready for the vote, that moral education must precede political enfranchisement, and that agitation for electoral reform serves the interests of demagogues more than the poor. He is, in other words, a radical who is deeply conservative — an argument that the novel advances with considerable intelligence and that has irritated readers on both left and right ever since.

The novel interweaves three plots. Felix Holt himself is a watchmaker who has deliberately renounced the comfortable life his father's patent medicine business might have provided, choosing instead to work with his hands and educate himself for what he believes to be a genuine rather than a meretricious radicalism. The heiress Esther Lyon, brought up in genteel poverty by a dissenting minister she later discovers is not her real father, must choose between Felix and the comfortable inheritance she has unexpectedly acquired. And around these central figures, Eliot constructs a legal and political plot of considerable complexity concerning the Transome estate — a plot that turns on the repressed secret of Harold Transome's illegitimate birth and the tragic figure of his mother Mrs. Transome, whose guilt and suffering constitute the novel's deepest emotional truth.

Mrs. Transome is one of the most powerful figures in Eliot's fiction, though she appears relatively infrequently. She has paid for her past with decades of internal suffering, and now faces the final indignity of watching her son — for whose sake she sinned — dismiss her experience and override her wishes with cheerful obliviousness. The scene in which she learns that her secret is known to Jermyn the solicitor, who had been her lover, is rendered with a compression and psychological intensity that few passages in Victorian fiction can match.

The historical setting — 1832, the year of the First Reform Act — allows Eliot to examine the limits of political solutions. Felix Holt's scepticism about electoral reform is not conservatism but a form of radicalism that looks beyond the mechanics of the franchise to the deeper question of what kind of society political change is supposed to produce. Eliot was herself deeply sceptical of the optimism surrounding the Reform agitation, and the novel's dramatic climax — a riot at Treby Magna on election day in which Felix, attempting to lead the mob away from violence, is arrested and tried for manslaughter — embodies her conviction that political passions, without moral grounding, produce destruction.

Felix Holt was Eliot's fourth novel, published after Romola's laborious composition and before the seven-year preparation for Middlemarch. It sold well initially, and it prompted Eliot to write a brief political essay, 'Address to Working Men, by Felix Holt,' published in Blackwood's Magazine in 1868 — a rare piece of direct political intervention that essentially extended Felix's argument into the debate over the Second Reform Act of 1867. The 1885 Cabinet Edition is the standard text, incorporating the revisions Eliot made for the 1878 collected edition.
contents: The Transome estate: Mrs. Transome's secret, Harold's return from Smyrna, and Jermyn the solicitor
Felix Holt's radicalism: moral education versus electoral agitation, and the limits of political reform
Esther Lyon's choice: inheritance, identity, and the education of a woman of feeling
The Treby Magna election riot: the novel's dramatic climax and Felix's arrest and trial
The historical context: the First Reform Act of 1832 and the transformation of English political society

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Seventh — Catalogue No. XXVII
books.index_title: Silas Marner — The Weaver of Raveloe
books.author: George Eliot
subtitle_lines: The Weaver of Raveloe
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXV. Cabinet Edition
essay: Silas Marner was published in April 1861, between The Mill on the Floss and Romola, and is in some ways the most perfect of Eliot's novels — a small-scale, concentrated work that achieves within its modest compass everything she was trying to do. The story of a linen-weaver, unjustly expelled from his Dissenting community and reduced to miserly isolation in the village of Raveloe, who finds his gold stolen and a golden-haired child left in its place — and through that child is gradually restored to human connection — has the structural clarity and moral force of a fable. It is also, underneath its pastoral surface, one of the most psychologically and philosophically serious novels Eliot wrote.

Silas Marner came to Eliot suddenly, she told her publisher, 'as a sort of legendary tale, suggested by my recollection of having once, in early childhood, seen a linen-weaver with a bag on his back.' The image generated a meditation on the relationship between religious community, individual consciousness, and the capacity for trust. Silas, driven from his community by a false accusation of theft, loses his faith in divine justice and replaces it with the mechanical accumulation of gold — a form of monomania that insulates him from human relationship as effectively as his exile has. The theft of the gold, by the wasted younger son of Squire Cass, strips him of this compensation and leaves him completely desolate.

The arrival of the infant Eppie — whose mother has died in the snow outside Silas's cottage — represents not a sentimental resolution but a second chance at exactly the trust that was taken from Silas. He chooses to keep her, raises her, and through her is gradually reintegrated into the village community. The novel traces this process with extraordinary precision: the specific steps by which a personality that has contracted into self-protection is opened out again by the demands of another. It is, in its quiet way, one of the great accounts of psychological healing in the literature.

The parallel plot concerns the Cass family and particularly Godfrey Cass, who knows that Eppie is his daughter and does nothing — a study in the moral cost of a comfortable cowardice that never quite becomes evil. His eventual confession to his wife Nancy, sixteen years too late, and the scene in which Eppie refuses his belated claim, is the novel's moral conclusion: that the ties of care and habit constitute a deeper parenthood than blood, and that the obligations we evade do not simply disappear but transform themselves into the shape of our worst fears.

Silas Marner has always been a favourite with readers, and was for a long time considered too simple and too optimistic to merit the serious critical attention given to Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda. This condescension has gradually receded. The novel's philosophical depth — its engagement with Feuerbach's ideas about the human basis of religious feeling, its understanding of community as a moral necessity rather than a social accident — is now more clearly recognised. The 1885 Cabinet Edition reprints the text Eliot revised for the 1878 collected edition. She regarded it with particular affection.
contents: Part I — Silas's exile: the false accusation at Lantern Yard, arrival in Raveloe, and the miser's gold
The Cass family: Godfrey's secret marriage, his brother Dunstan's theft, and the Squire's household
The arrival of Eppie: the child in the snow, Silas's choice, and the beginning of recovery
Part II — Sixteen years on: Eppie grown; Godfrey's confession; and Eppie's refusal of her father's claim
The philosophical background: Feuerbach, religious community, and the human basis of trust

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Eighth — Catalogue No. XXVIII
books.index_title: The Coming Race
books.author: Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton
subtitle_lines: Also published as: Vril — the Power of the Coming Race
edition_lines: Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton, First Baron Lytton
books.imprint: Published by William Blackwood and Sons — Edinburgh and London, MDCCCLXXXVI
essay: The Coming Race was first published anonymously in May 1871 by Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and London, and was Bulwer-Lytton's penultimate novel, appearing just two years before his death. It is the strangest work in his long and varied career: not the silver-fork comedy or the Newgate thriller or the historical romance of his previous decades but a work of speculative fiction — one of the first in the English language — in which a nameless young American descends through a mine shaft into a subterranean world inhabited by an advanced humanoid race called the Vril-ya. The 1886 edition held in this library is a posthumous reprint of a novel that had been continuously in print since its anonymous first appearance.

The Vril-ya take their name from Vril — 'an all-permeating fluid,' as Bulwer-Lytton's narrator describes it, which Faraday might call atmospheric magnetism and which the Vril-ya have learned to harness for purposes of creation, healing, and destruction. A child among the Vril-ya, wielding a Vril staff, can casually destroy anything that threatens the community. This total parity of destructive capability has produced a society without war, without crime, and without government in any form familiar to surface-dwellers. It has also produced, by Bulwer-Lytton's satirical logic, a society that has outgrown democracy — the word the Vril-ya use for democracy, Koom-Posh, translates roughly as 'the government of the ignorant majority.'

The novel is simultaneously a utopia and a warning. The Vril-ya are admirable in many respects: their gender relations are, by Victorian standards, remarkably equal; their technology is extraordinary; their social peace is genuine. But they are also cold, inhuman in their impassive capacity for destruction, and — most disturbingly — planning eventually to rise to the surface and displace or destroy the degenerate surface races. The narrator's urgency, at the novel's end, is that of a man who has seen the future and found it terrifying precisely because it is so superior. He was allowed to escape only because the Vril-ya woman who loved him chose exile over his death.

The novel's afterlife has been peculiar. Bovril, the British yeast extract introduced in the 1870s, takes its name from a combination of 'Bo' (from Latin bos, meaning ox) and 'Vril' — evidence of how quickly the fictional energy-fluid entered the popular imagination. Helena Blavatsky, founder of Theosophy, cited Vril as evidence for real occult forces; Rudolf Steiner and other esotericists followed her. A 1960 French book, The Morning of the Magicians, suggested that a real 'Vril Society' had existed in Weimar Berlin, a claim that passed into the murkier reaches of twentieth-century mythology. Bulwer-Lytton himself, in a letter to John Forster, was precise about his meaning: 'I did not mean Vril for mesmerism, but for electricity, developed into uses as yet only dimly guessed.'

Edward Bulwer-Lytton (1803–1873) was one of the most commercially successful and critically derided writers of the Victorian period — a man whose phrase 'It was a dark and stormy night' has become the byword for bad prose. This reputation is somewhat unfair, particularly to his later work, of which The Coming Race is the most interesting example. It was written, as all his later novels were, in shorter compass than the three-volume productions of his youth, and the compression suits him. Its influence on subsequent science fiction — on H. G. Wells, H. Rider Haggard, and the hollow-earth tradition generally — was considerable and is still not fully acknowledged.
contents: The descent: a mine shaft, a dead companion, and the discovery of the underground world
The Vril-ya: their history, their technology, and the all-pervasive force of Vril
Society without government: how total destructive capability produces civilised peace
Gender reversed: Vril-ya women as the dominant sex, and the narrator's dangerous attractiveness
The warning: the Vril-ya's eventual plan to surface and displace or destroy humanity

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-First — Catalogue No. LXI
books.index_title: Wild Life and Adventure in the Australian Bush
books.author: Arthur Nicols
subtitle_lines: Four Years' Personal Experience
edition_lines: Author of 'The Acclimatisation of the Salmonidae at the Antipodes'
books.imprint: Printed for Richard Bentley and Son, Publishers in Ordinary to Her Majesty — London, MDCCCLXXXVII
essay: Wild Life and Adventure in the Australian Bush is the record of four years spent by a working naturalist on the far side of the world, and it belongs to that distinctively Victorian genre in which sport, travel and serious natural history are bound together between the same covers. Published by Richard Bentley and Son in 1887 in two volumes, it is neither a scientific monograph nor a mere traveller's diary but something between the two: the testimony of a man who went to Australia with his eyes open and a collector's instincts intact, and who came back with both specimens and stories.

The book moves between the drawing-room and the campfire. Nicols describes the marsupials, birds and reptiles of the colony with the precision of someone who has handled them, and the bush itself — its heat, its silences, its sudden violence — with the relish of someone who has slept in it. There are hunting episodes, encounters with settlers and with Aboriginal Australians, and long passages of patient observation. The modern reader will feel the familiar Victorian tension on every page: genuine wonder at a fauna found nowhere else on earth, set beside the casual, gun-in-hand destructiveness that the age took entirely for granted. Nicols is a more careful observer than most of his sporting contemporaries, but he is a man of his time, and the book is the more revealing for it.

Running beneath the adventures is Nicols's abiding preoccupation: acclimatisation — the Victorian project of remaking the ecologies of the colonies in the image of home. He had written a whole treatise on the introduction of salmon and trout to the Antipodes, and the question of what European species might be made to flourish in Australia, and at what cost to what was already there, is never far from his mind. Read today, the book is an unintentional document of an ecological catastrophe in the making: the rabbits, the foxes, the displacement of native species — all of it implicit in the confident improving spirit Nicols shared with his contemporaries.

Of Arthur Nicols himself the record is thin. He was a Victorian naturalist and prolific science writer rather than a gentleman of independent means, earning his living by the pen across a range of subjects: Chapters from the Physical History of the Earth (1880), The Acclimatisation of the Salmonidae at the Antipodes (1882), and Natural History Sketches among the Carnivora (1885) among them. He moved in scientific circles and is listed among the many correspondents of Charles Darwin. He belongs to the large, now mostly forgotten company of competent Victorian naturalists who did the unglamorous work of observing, recording and popularising, in the long shadow cast by the great theorists of the age.

It is a less celebrated book than most of its neighbours on these shelves, and that is rather the point of its being here. A library made only of acknowledged masterpieces would be a poorer and less honest thing. This is a working naturalist's eyewitness account of a particular place at a particular moment — the Australian colonial frontier as the nineteenth century found it, and began, without quite understanding what it was doing, to remake it. The text survives, scanned and freely available; the book — handled, illustrated, bound by Bentley for a Victorian reader's shelf — survives here, which is a different and better kind of survival.
contents: Four years' personal experience in the Australian bush
Observations of the marsupials, birds and reptiles of the colony
The acclimatisation question — European species introduced to the Antipodes
Sporting and hunting episodes of the colonial frontier
Encounters with settlers and with Aboriginal Australians
Numerous illustrations; published in two volumes by Richard Bentley and Son

books.eyebrow: Entry the Twenty-Ninth, Thirtieth & Thirty-First — Catalogue No. XXIX–XXXI
books.index_title: The Parent's Cabinet of Amusement and Instruction (3 vols.)
books.author: Ed. Martha Hill
title_lines: The Parent's Cabinet of Amusement and Instruction
subtitle_lines: Three Volumes
edition_lines: Edited by Martha Hill — with contributions from Various Authors
books.imprint: Published by Smith, Elder and Company — London, MDCCCLXXXIX
essay: The Parent's Cabinet of Amusement and Instruction was a long-lived Victorian miscellany for children, first published by Smith, Elder and Company in the mid-1830s and reprinted in numerous editions across the following half-century. This library holds three volumes of the 1889 edition, attributed to Martha Hill as editor — though as was common with such publications, the editorship was understood to be a curatorial function, the individual authorship of articles and stories being largely suppressed in favour of the collective identity of the Cabinet itself. The title captures the central aspiration of Victorian children's publishing in one phrase: amusement and instruction, pleasure and improvement, simultaneously and inseparably pursued.

The contents of any given volume of the Cabinet are a characteristic sampling of mid-Victorian juvenile literature: short tales of moral instruction in which well-behaved children are rewarded and poorly-behaved ones suffer appropriate consequences; biographical sketches of notable men of science, exploration, or religious virtue suitable for young readers; articles on natural history presenting the wonders of creation as evidence of divine benevolence; geographical sketches of distant lands and peoples; and interspersed puzzles, verses, and simple domestic arts. The wood-engraved illustrations that accompany the text are in the solid tradition of Victorian children's book illustration — clear, informative, and slightly stiff.

Smith, Elder and Company was one of the major Victorian publishers, responsible for the first editions of many significant works including Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre and Villette, Thackeray's contributions to the Cornhill Magazine (which Smith, Elder also published), and later the works of John Ruskin and Elizabeth Barrett Browning. The house had a particular commitment to literature of quality and a serious editorial standard. That a publisher of this standing produced the Parent's Cabinet across several decades is a reminder that juvenile literature was not a marginal concern for Victorian publishers but a substantial and commercially important part of their output.

The editor named on these volumes, Martha Hill, belongs to the large company of Victorian women who sustained the children's literature trade through editorial, didactic, and narrative work that was professionally competent, socially useful, and almost entirely anonymous. The names of individual contributors to collections of this kind were rarely preserved in bibliographic records; the texts were regarded as instruments of education rather than works of individual literary art. This attitude has made the recovery of the lives and careers of such editors and contributors extremely difficult for subsequent scholars.

Three volumes of the Parent's Cabinet sitting together in an Irish library in 1889 are most naturally imagined as a gift — the kind of serious, improving gift that Victorian and Edwardian families gave to children whose education they wished to encourage. The books are not novels to be read privately in an evening but a resource to be consulted, enjoyed a chapter at a time, and returned to. They represent a particular theory of childhood: that children benefit from guided exposure to good narrative and reliable information, that the domestic setting of parental supervision is the right context for such exposure, and that the combination of pleasure and instruction is not merely commercially convenient but pedagogically sound.
contents: Tales of moral instruction: stories of honesty, industry, kindness, and the consequences of their opposites
Biographical sketches: lives of men of science, exploration, and religious virtue suitable for young readers
Natural history articles: the wonders of creation presented as evidence of providential design
Geographical sketches: distant lands and peoples, framed for the improvement of young minds
Wood-engraved illustrations throughout; publisher's advertisements for the Smith, Elder children's list

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Second — Catalogue No. XXXII
books.index_title: Haydn's Dictionary of Dates — Nineteenth Edition
books.author: Benjamin Vincent
title_lines: Haydn's Dictionary of Dates and Universal Information
subtitle_lines: Relating to All Ages and Nations — Nineteenth Edition
edition_lines: Edited by Benjamin Vincent, Librarian of the Royal Institution
books.imprint: Published by Ward, Lock and Company — London, New York and Melbourne, MDCCCLXXXIX
essay: Haydn's Dictionary of Dates is one of the great Victorian reference books — a single-volume compendium of historical chronology, biography, geography, and miscellaneous fact, organised alphabetically and cross-referenced so that the reader who wished to know the date of the Battle of Actium, the founding of the Bank of England, the publication of Paradise Lost, or the elevation of every Archbishop of Canterbury since the Reformation could find it without resort to any other source. First compiled by Joseph Haydn (c.1786–1856) and published in 1841, it went through edition after edition across the rest of the century. This nineteenth edition contains the history of the world to the autumn of 1889.

The Dictionary covers events from ancient and modern kingdoms alike, offering chronological tables within subject headings — Battles, Earthquakes, Inventions, Literature, Parliaments, Wars — alongside biographical entries and geographical notes. Its format rewards browsing as much as consultation: the reader who opens it at random will find, within a few columns, the date of the invention of the microscope, the succession of Ottoman sultans, and the principal eruptions of Vesuvius. In a period before the encyclopaedia had reached its modern form, Haydn filled a genuine gap in the Victorian reference library.

Benjamin Vincent (1818–1899) took over the editorship and expanded it through multiple editions, keeping it current with each new printing and adding material on the accelerating events of the latter half of the nineteenth century — the revolutions of 1848, the American Civil War, the Franco-Prussian War, the Scramble for Africa. He served as assistant secretary and later librarian of the Royal Institution of Great Britain from 1848 to 1889, which gave him access to the finest scientific minds of the day.

The nineteenth edition runs to over a thousand pages in double column — a volume of formidable weight and considerable utility. The Victorian educated class kept it to hand as a matter of course, in the same way they kept a dictionary and an atlas: a permanent resident of the desk, consulted the moment a date became doubtful or a name unfamiliar. Its authority derived not from any single author's scholarship but from the accumulated editorial intelligence of half a century of revision.

This 1889 edition was published simultaneously in London, New York, and Melbourne — an index of the book's reach across the English-speaking world. Ward, Lock and Company, who published it, were one of the principal Victorian popular reference publishers, responsible among other things for an early edition of Enquire Within Upon Everything. Haydn and Ward Lock together represent the Victorian conviction that all useful knowledge could, with sufficient editorial industry, be brought within a single volume.
contents: Chronological tables: Battles, Earthquakes, Inventions, Parliaments, Sieges, and Wars across all recorded history
Biographical entries: monarchs, statesmen, philosophers, scientists, and military commanders
Geographical notes: countries, cities, and principal landmarks from ancient to modern times
Addenda: events of 1888–89 supplementing the main alphabetical body
Index of principal persons and subjects

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Third — Catalogue No. XXXIII
books.index_title: The Poetical Works of Sir Walter Scott
books.author: Sir Walter Scott
title_lines: The Poetical Works of Sir Walter Scott
books.imprint: Published 1895
essay: Walter Scott's poetry belongs to the first phase of his literary life — the decade between 1805 and 1815 when he was the most popular poet in Britain. The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805), Marmion (1808), and The Lady of the Lake (1810) were each received with an enthusiasm that their author later found difficult to credit. The Lady of the Lake sold twenty-five thousand copies in eight months. These were cultural events, read aloud in drawing rooms, memorised by schoolchildren, and treated as expressions of national feeling.

The poems are long narrative works in the tradition of the Romantic verse romance — energetic, melodious, and saturated with the Border country Scott had loved since childhood. They are built on ballad forms and ballad subjects: border feuds, clan loyalties, tournaments, and sieges, all rendered in octosyllabic couplets that move with the speed of a horse. Scott had immersed himself in the ballad tradition through his great collection Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802–03), and the poems that followed draw on that immersion deeply.

The decline of Scott's poetic reputation in his own lifetime was something he accepted with characteristic good grace. Byron appeared and swept him from the market; Scott acknowledged it cheerfully. He turned to prose and discovered his true genius — but the verse romances retain the energy of a young man discovering his powers, writing at white heat about a landscape he inhabited with his whole imaginative being. They are not subtle, but they are alive.

Scott (1771–1832) was born in Edinburgh, raised partly in the Border country, educated at Edinburgh University, and appointed Sheriff of Selkirkshire in 1799. His literary career ran concurrently with his grandiose project of building Abbotsford, the great house on the Tweed that became both his pride and his financial ruin. The collapse of Constable in 1826 left him with debts of over £120,000. He spent the last six years of his life writing to pay them off, and very nearly succeeded.

A collected Poetical Works has been a standard fixture of the Victorian and Edwardian library since the middle of the century. The shorter poems — 'Lochinvar,' 'Breathes there the man,' the songs from the novels — remained in every anthology and on every schoolroom wall. The long poems are less read today than they were, but they remain the record of a moment when narrative verse could command the largest audience in the English-speaking world.
contents: The Lay of the Last Minstrel (1805): the story of Lady Margaret and the magic book
Marmion (1808): the Battle of Flodden Field and its antecedents
The Lady of the Lake (1810): Loch Katrine, Roderick Dhu, and the Fiery Cross
The shorter poems: songs from the novels, ballads, and occasional verse
Introductory memoir and notes on the composition of the principal works

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Fourth — Catalogue No. XXXIV
books.index_title: The Second Jungle Book
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.imprint: Published by Macmillan and Company — London, 1903 edition
essay: The Second Jungle Book appeared in 1895, completing Kipling's extraordinary double act of imaginative world-building. It adds the Red Dog — the Dholes who pour into the jungle like a red tide — and gives Mowgli the grandest of his adventures: the hunting of the Dholes with the Little People of the Rock. It also adds stories outside the Mowgli cycle: 'The Miracle of Purun Bhagat,' a former prime minister who renounces power; and 'The Spring Running,' the most elegiac of all, in which the young man-cub finally leaves the jungle for the world of men.

Kipling (1865–1936) conceived the Mowgli stories in Vermont, during the years of his marriage to Caroline Balestier, when he was as far from India as he had ever been. The distance seems to have intensified the imaginative possession: 'The pen took charge,' he wrote later, 'and I watched it begin to write stories about Mowgli and the animals.' His father John Lockwood Kipling contributed both corrections and illustrations to the first book.

The Law of the Jungle — Kipling's elaboration of the unwritten code by which the animals govern themselves — is one of the more resonant inventions of Victorian children's literature, functioning simultaneously as a guide to pack behaviour, an allegory of imperial administration, and a template for boyhood virtue. 'For the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the strength of the Wolf is the Pack' is the kind of aphorism that sounds like a folk proverb but was written by a single hand.

The 1903 Macmillan edition is one of many that kept the Jungle Books continuously in print. By 1903 the books were already established as classics of their kind, read simultaneously by children who loved the adventure and by adults who heard the deeper harmonics. Kipling received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907.

The Mowgli cycle as a whole represents one of the great sustained feats of imaginative creation in English prose. Mowgli's final departure from the jungle at the end of 'The Spring Running' has the quality of genuine loss: not just of a character from a setting, but of a whole way of being in the world that the stories had made seem, briefly, possible.
contents: How Fear Came: the drought at the Peace Rock and the origin of the Law of the Jungle
The Miracle of Purun Bhagat: a former prime minister becomes a holy man — and saves a village
Red Dog: Mowgli's alliance with the bees against the Dhole pack
The Spring Running: Mowgli's farewell to the jungle and passage into the world of men
Outsong: the final poem, spoken in chorus by Baloo, Bagheera, Kaa, and the Jungle

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Fifth — Catalogue No. XXXV
books.index_title: The Life of Nelson
books.author: Robert Southey
books.imprint: Published 1903 edition
essay: The Life of Nelson is the most famous biography in the English language of its period, and one of the small number of Victorian prose works that can be said to have had a direct influence on events. Published in 1813, eight years after Trafalgar, it was received as the definitive account of Britain's greatest naval hero — written with a poet's gift for narrative and a moralist's concern for character. The American government thought it so useful as an example to seamen that it issued a copy to every officer in the United States Navy.

Southey set out, in his own preface, to write a life 'clear and concise enough to become a manual for the young sailor, which he may carry about with him till he has treasured it up for example in his memory and in his heart.' The book is short — barely three hundred pages — and moves with the speed that a poet brings to narrative. The great set-pieces — the Nile, Copenhagen, Trafalgar, and Nelson's death — are rendered with a vividness that no subsequent biographer has quite managed to surpass in so compact a space.

Southey treats Nelson's affair with Lady Hamilton with the distaste of a man of his class and age, and his account of Nelson's private character is shaped by this moral framework. But his account of Nelson as a naval commander, as a leader of men, and as a figure whose courage and cheerful exposure to danger inspired those around him is analytically precise. He understood what made Nelson irreplaceable: the combination of technical mastery and personal magnetism that is rarer than genius alone.

Robert Southey (1774–1843) is now remembered chiefly as a Poet Laureate who outlasted his own reputation and the author of 'The Battle of Blenheim.' He was also a serious historian and biographer. His Life of Nelson is a case where a lesser literary reputation has attached itself to a more lasting book: the biography outlived the poet by more than a century.

This 1903 edition is one of many reprints produced across the Victorian and Edwardian period. Trafalgar was within living memory of men born in the 1790s; by 1903 it had passed into history, but Southey's Life kept the human reality of Nelson alive in the face of the gradual monumentalisation of the man into mere myth.
contents: Nelson's early life: Norfolk boyhood, his uncle's patronage, first sea service
The Battle of the Nile, 1798: the destruction of the French fleet and Nelson's rise to fame
Copenhagen, 1801: the telescope to the blind eye and the destruction of the Danish fleet
Trafalgar, 21 October 1805: 'England expects...'; the final battle and Nelson's death
Character and legacy: Southey's assessment of Nelson's qualities as commander and man

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Sixth — Catalogue No. XXXVI
books.index_title: Histoire de la Litterature Francaise — Vol. I
books.author: Emile Faguet
subtitle_lines: Volume I — Des Origines jusqu'au XVIIe Siecle
books.imprint: Publie par Plon-Nourrit et Compagnie — Paris, MDCCCCV. Illustree d'apres les manuscrits de la Bibliotheque nationale
essay: Emile Faguet's Histoire de la litterature francaise is the standard popular history of French literature from the early twentieth century — comprehensive, beautifully illustrated, and written with the authority of a man who had spent his career as the leading literary critic of the Revue Bleue and the Journal des debats. Published in two volumes between 1900 and 1905 by Plon-Nourrit, it covers French literature from its origins in the chanson de geste through the Renaissance. Volume I ends at the threshold of the grand siecle — with Montaigne, Ronsard, and the Pleiade.

The first volume traces the extraordinary flowering of medieval French literature — the Chansons de Roland, the romans courtois, the poetry of the troubadours — through the Renaissance rediscovery of classical antiquity and the formation of the French language as a literary instrument. The Pleiade — Ronsard, du Bellay, and their companions — receive particular attention as the moment when French poetry first declared its ambition to rival the ancients on their own terms.

Emile Faguet (1847–1916) was born at La Roche-sur-Yon, educated at the Ecole normale superieure, and rose to become professor of poetry at the Sorbonne and a member of the Academie francaise, elected in 1900. He was an extraordinarily prolific critic — the author of studies on Corneille, Racine, Voltaire, Rousseau, Flaubert, Balzac, and dozens of others, as well as political works including The Cult of Incompetence (1911).

The illustrations are one of the great attractions of this edition — reproductions from manuscripts and prints held in the Bibliotheque nationale, showing illuminated medieval texts, portraits of Renaissance authors, and title pages of first editions. The visual record of French literary history is presented with the same care that the text brings to the literary record.

That two volumes of Faguet should appear in an Irish library in 1905 and 1909 is entirely natural. French was the first language of educated Europe, and the Irish educated class of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries read French literature as a matter of course. The Abbey Theatre's founders were steeped in French symbolism; Yeats and George Moore both spoke and read French with ease.
contents: The chansons de geste: Roland, Guillaume d'Orange, and the epic tradition of medieval France
The romans courtois: Chretien de Troyes, Tristan, and the literature of courtly love
The troubadours and trouveres: lyric poetry and the formation of the vernacular tradition
The Renaissance: Marot, Rabelais, and the encounter with classical antiquity
The Pleiade: Ronsard, du Bellay, and the Defence and Illustration of the French Language

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Seventh — Catalogue No. XXXVII
books.index_title: The Works of William Shakespeare — Vol. II: Histories
books.author: William Shakespeare
title_lines: The Works of William Shakespeare in Three Volumes
subtitle_lines: Volume II: The Histories
books.imprint: Published 1905
essay: A collected Shakespeare in three volumes, arranged by genre, is the standard Victorian and Edwardian format for presenting the plays to a general readership. Volume II, containing the Histories, is in one sense the most distinctively English of the three: these are plays that grow directly from the national past, drawing on Holinshed's Chronicles to dramatise the crises of medieval kingship from Richard II through Henry VIII, giving that past a vividness and moral seriousness that no subsequent dramatist has equalled.

The English History plays form one of the greatest sustained projects in literary history. Shakespeare wrote them intermittently across a decade, with no systematic plan we can reconstruct, but the result has the coherence of a great design: the fall of Richard II, the usurpation of Bolingbroke, the long penance of the Lancastrian line, the triumph of Henry V, the dissolution under Henry VI, and the nightmare of Richard III — all linked by a vision of history as a moral process in which the sins of kings are paid for across generations.

Henry IV Parts 1 and 2 are arguably the greatest of the histories. The Falstaff scenes are the richest comic writing in the language, and the political scenes between Hal and his father are among the most psychologically penetrating. Richard II reads like a lyric poem dramatised; Richard III like a devil's autobiography. Henry V is the most debated — read as sincere patriotic celebration and as savage irony, sometimes simultaneously.

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, educated at the local grammar school, and established in London as actor and playwright by the early 1590s. The History plays were among the most popular in his own time, drawing on a knowledge of the national past that his audiences shared and a capacity for political drama that touched the anxieties of an Elizabethan England preoccupied with succession and legitimacy.

The 1905 date places this volume at the height of the Edwardian Shakespeare revival — a period when the History plays were being reread in the context of Britain's imperial moment. Henry V was recruited as a text of national purpose. Subsequent decades complicated this reading severely. The plays' power to absorb and reflect the preoccupations of each new age is itself evidence of their depth.
contents: Richard II: the deposition of a poet-king and the origin of the Lancastrian line
Henry IV Parts 1 and 2: Falstaff, Hotspur, Hal, and the education of a prince
Henry V: Agincourt, the St Crispin's Day speech, and the ambiguities of heroic kingship
The Henry VI trilogy and Richard III: the Wars of the Roses and the rise of the last Plantagenet
Henry VIII: Wolsey's fall, Cranmer's triumph, and the birth of Elizabeth

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Eighth — Catalogue No. XXXVIII
books.index_title: The Poetical Works of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
books.author: H. W. Longfellow
title_lines: The Poetical Works of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
books.imprint: Published 1907
essay: Longfellow was, in the 1860s and 1870s, the most widely read poet in the English-speaking world — a statement that requires historical imagination to credit, but was simply true. His popularity in Britain exceeded even that of Tennyson in certain social strata. By 1907, when this edition was published, his reputation had begun the long decline that would reach its nadir in the mid-twentieth century, but his works remained standard fixtures of the schoolroom and the parlour.
