The poems on which his fame rested were above all the long narratives: Evangeline (1847), a tale of Acadian exile in hexameters; The Song of Hiawatha (1855), retelling the legends of the Ojibwe people in a metre from the Finnish Kalevala; and The Courtship of Miles Standish (1858), a comedy of colonial New England. Of these, Hiawatha was the most celebrated and most parodied — its trochaic octameter ('By the shores of Gitche Gumee') became so familiar that it needed only to be reproduced to produce laughter.

The shorter poems kept a more durable reputation: 'A Psalm of Life,' 'The Village Blacksmith,' 'Paul Revere's Ride,' 'Excelsior,' and 'The Arrow and the Song' were among the most anthologised poems in English through the Victorian and Edwardian periods. They embodied a Victorian conception of what poetry was for that the modernist movement would later find embarrassing, but which served a genuine social function.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882) was born in Portland, Maine, educated at Bowdoin College, and spent most of his professional life as Professor of Modern Languages at Harvard. He was America's first great professional man of letters in the European sense — a scholar-poet who translated Dante and edited collections of European poetry. His personal life was marked by tragedy: his second wife was killed in a fire in 1861, an event from which he never fully recovered.

The 1907 Poetical Works is one of the innumerable British editions that kept Longfellow in print. His influence on Irish literary culture was particular: Thomas Davis and the Young Ireland movement drew on his example for their belief in the political power of poetry addressed to a popular audience, and his work was taught in the national schools alongside Moore's Melodies as an example of what poetry could do for a national consciousness.
contents: Evangeline (1847): Acadian exile and reunion, told in classical hexameters
The Song of Hiawatha (1855): Ojibwe legend retold in Kalevala metre
The Courtship of Miles Standish (1858): Pilgrim colonial comedy in three cantos
The shorter poems: 'A Psalm of Life', 'Paul Revere's Ride', 'Excelsior', and the parlour classics
The Divine Tragedy and other later works; translations from Dante

books.eyebrow: Entry the Thirty-Ninth — Catalogue No. XXXIX
books.index_title: Histoire de la Litterature Francaise — Vol. II
books.author: Emile Faguet
subtitle_lines: Volume II — Depuis le XVIIe Siecle jusqu'a Nos Jours
books.imprint: Publie par Plon-Nourrit et Compagnie — Paris, MDCCCCIX. Illustree d'apres les manuscrits de la Bibliotheque nationale
essay: The second volume of Faguet's Histoire covers the period from the grand siecle of Louis XIV to the threshold of the twentieth century — the Corneille-Racine-Moliere constellation, the Enlightenment, Romanticism, and the realist and naturalist schools of the nineteenth century. It is the volume that required the greatest critical discrimination, since the proximity of the material made impartiality harder and the abundance of significant names made compression more painful. Faguet manages it with the confident sweep of a man who had spent thirty years writing about almost every figure on these pages.

The classical theatre receives its due: Faguet is especially good on Racine, whose psychological precision he admires and whose formal rigour he regards as the definitive expression of the French classical genius. The Enlightenment — Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu, the Encyclopedistes — is handled with characteristic ambivalence: admiration for the wit and clarity of the philosophes, suspicion of their social consequences.

The nineteenth century presents Faguet with the full range of his critical strengths and limitations. He is excellent on the Romantics — Hugo's colossal energy, Lamartine's lyric melancholy, Alfred de Vigny's aristocratic pessimism — and on the realists Stendhal and Balzac. He is less comfortable with the Naturalists — Zola's documentation of working-class life sits uneasily with his classical formation — and his treatment of Baudelaire and the Symbolists is noticeably cooler.

Emile Faguet (1847–1916) was among the most widely read literary critics in France at the turn of the century — his weekly feuilletons for the Journal des debats reached a mass readership. He died in Paris in 1916, having seen the country he had written about so extensively plunged into the catastrophe that would end the world he knew.

The two volumes of Faguet in this library — 1905 and 1909 — cover French literature comprehensively from the medieval period to the early twentieth century. Together they constitute a complete literary education in a tradition that the Irish literary revival was simultaneously drawing on and reacting against: Yeats and the Symbolists, Synge's debt to French realism, Moore's years in Paris among the Impressionists.
contents: The grand siecle: Corneille, Racine, Moliere, and the classical theatre of Louis XIV
The Enlightenment: Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu, and the Encyclopedie
Romanticism: Hugo, Lamartine, Vigny, Musset, and the Romantic revolution
Realism and Naturalism: Stendhal, Balzac, Flaubert, and Zola
The Symbolists: Baudelaire, Verlaine, Rimbaud, and the poetry of the late nineteenth century

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fortieth — Catalogue No. XL
books.index_title: Just So Stories for Little Children
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
title_lines: Just So Stories for Little Children
books.imprint: Published by Macmillan and Company — London, 1910 edition
essay: Just So Stories was first published by Macmillan in 1902 — a collection of twelve origin myths, told in a voice of elaborate mock-solemnity, explaining how the camel got his hump, how the rhinoceros got his skin, how the elephant got his trunk. The stories were told orally, over many years, to his daughter Josephine, who died of pneumonia in 1899 at the age of six. The book carries her absence in its pages as a kind of silent grief.

The prose style is entirely unlike anything else Kipling wrote — deliberately archaic, densely repetitive, full of invented proper names ('the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees') and ceremonious qualifications ('my Best Beloved,' 'O Best Beloved'), designed to be read aloud with full performative commitment. The rhythm is incantatory; the comedy depends on a narrative voice that maintains perfect gravity while advancing propositions of perfect absurdity.

Kipling illustrated the first edition himself, with drawings that are both eccentric and completely apt — the elephant's trunk elongated by the crocodile, the rhinoceros's skin crumpled by cake-crumbs, the crab whose shell is inscribed with marks. The drawings extend and comment on the text rather than merely illustrating it, and have the quality of marginalia in an ancient manuscript.

Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907 — the first English-language writer to do so — and was at various points the most widely read writer in the English language. The Just So Stories belong to a period when he was living at Bateman's in Sussex, farming, gardening, and writing with a domestic contentment that the Boer War and Josephine's death had made hard-won.

The 1910 Macmillan edition is one of many reprints following the book's immediate success. The Just So Stories entered the language almost immediately: 'the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo' became a byword for a particular kind of magnificent prose excess, and the stories themselves entered the repertoire of every parent who read aloud to children. They remain there.
contents: How the Whale Got His Throat; How the Camel Got His Hump; How the Rhinoceros Got His Skin
How the Leopard Got His Spots; The Elephant's Child; The Sing-Song of Old Man Kangaroo
The Beginning of the Armadilloes; How the First Letter Was Written; How the Alphabet Was Made
The Crab That Played with the Sea; The Cat That Walked by Himself; The Butterfly That Stamped
Kipling's own illustrations: drawings by the author, eccentric, authoritative, and inseparable from the text

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-First — Catalogue No. XLI
books.index_title: A Diversity of Creatures
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.imprint: Published by Macmillan and Company — London, 1925 edition
essay: A Diversity of Creatures was first published in 1917, collecting fourteen stories that had appeared in various magazines between 1911 and 1917. It belongs to the later Kipling, the writer who had survived the death of his son John at Loos in 1915 and whose work was increasingly preoccupied with grief, damage, and the difficulty of healing. The collection contains some of his finest stories, among them 'Mary Postgate,' the most disturbing story he ever wrote, and 'The Village that Voted the Earth Was Flat,' the funniest.

The range of the collection is characteristic of Kipling's mature manner — tonal and formal variety within a collection unified by the author's intelligence and moral seriousness. 'Mary Postgate' is a study of controlled hatred finding release through a dying German airman — a story whose meaning remains contested after a century, deliberately so. 'The Village that Voted the Earth Was Flat' is a comedy of revenge through journalism and the music hall, building to a satirical denouement of surpassing skill.

The outbreak of war in 1914 had vindicated Kipling's warnings about German militarism. But the vindication brought no pleasure. He had used his influence to help his son John obtain a commission in the Irish Guards despite John's poor eyesight; John was reported missing at Loos in September 1915 and never found. His poem 'Common Form,' from Epitaphs of the War, reads: 'If any question why we died, / Tell them, because our fathers lied.' It is among the most savage epitaphs in the language.

By 1925, when this edition was published, Kipling's popular reputation had declined sharply from its pre-war peak. The political opinions that had made him the unofficial laureate of empire were now, in the aftermath of the war that had broken that empire's self-confidence, a liability rather than an asset. He was attacked from the left, condescended to by modernists.

The posthumous rehabilitation of Kipling — conducted by T. S. Eliot, who edited a selection of his poems in 1941 — has restored his standing without resolving the tension between his literary gifts and his political positions. A Diversity of Creatures sits at the fulcrum of that tension: published during the war he had helped bring about, containing stories that anatomise comedy and tragedy with equal precision.
contents: 'Mary Postgate': a spinster cares for a dying German airman — the most disturbing story Kipling wrote
'The Village that Voted the Earth Was Flat': journalism, music hall, and a comedy of perfect revenge
'In the Same Boat': two strangers bound by recurring nightmares and a common pre-natal origin
'Regulus': a Horace lesson at a boys' school — Kipling on empire, education, and the classics
The verse interludes: poems accompanying each story, often elaborating or ironising its meaning

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Second — Catalogue No. XLII
books.index_title: In Search of Ireland
books.author: H. V. Morton
books.imprint: Published by Methuen and Company — London, MDCCCXXX
essay: In Search of Ireland appeared in 1930, the latest in H. V. Morton's 'In Search of...' travel books. Morton had toured Ireland by motor car in the late 1920s, barely a decade after the War of Independence and the Treaty of 1921. The book he produced is both a vivid account of a country in the first years of its independence and a sustained act of sympathetic attention to a culture that English readers had been taught to regard with incomprehension or condescension.

The structure is that of a motor tour: Dublin first, then south and west through Wicklow, Tipperary, and Kerry, around Connemara, north to Donegal and the border, back through Ulster. Morton attends a wake in Mayo, visits Croagh Patrick, watches the harvest on a Connemara island, and drinks in a great many pubs. He has conversations with characters who are vivid, particular, and rooted in a tradition of oral performance that Morton recognises and responds to.

Morton brought to Ireland the same gifts that had made his English books successful: a sharp eye for landscape and architecture, an ability to compress historical information into narrative, and a prose style that is accessible without being condescending. He is particularly good on the west of Ireland — the quality of light in Connemara, the drama of the Dingle Peninsula, the strangeness of the Aran Islands.

Henry Canova Vollam Morton (1892–1979) was a journalist who had made his name scooping the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1923 and who reinvented himself as a travel writer. The posthumous discovery, through his private diaries, that he held Nazi sympathies has complicated his reputation. The travel books remain readable; the man behind them was more complex and less pleasant than they suggest.

In Search of Ireland is particularly interesting as a document of Irish self-presentation in the early years of the Free State — a new state of barely nine years, still deciding what kind of Ireland it wished to be. Morton responded warmly, and his book became one of the earliest successful pieces of heritage tourism: an invitation to the English-speaking world to discover Ireland as a place of beauty, depth, and human richness.
contents: Dublin: the Liffey, Trinity College, the Book of Kells, and the ghosts of 1916
The west: Connemara, the Aran Islands, and the persistence of Gaelic culture
Kerry: the Ring of Kerry, the lakes of Killarney, and the landscape of the south-west
The north: crossing the border into Ulster and the different Ireland of the six counties
Historical interludes: Norse settlers, medieval monasteries, Cromwell, the Penal Laws, and the Famine

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Third — Catalogue No. XLIII
books.index_title: On Forsyte 'Change
books.author: John Galsworthy
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, MDCCCXXX
essay: On Forsyte 'Change is a collection of short stories published in 1930, returning to the world of the Forsyte Saga for a final time. The Forsyte Saga itself — The Man of Property (1906), In Chancery (1920), and To Let (1921) — had been republished as a single volume in 1922 and become one of the great popular successes of the interwar period. On Forsyte 'Change gathered shorter pieces about the Forsyte family, filling in episodes from lives the novels had touched on briefly.

The Forsytes are Galsworthy's great creation — a family of prosperous late-Victorian solicitors and businessmen whose defining characteristic is their sense of property: their instinct to own, to possess, to convert everything, including people and beauty, into permanent holdings. Their world is rendered from inside with a sympathy that is always under ironic pressure — Galsworthy knew these people, belonged to their class, and understood exactly what they gained and lost by being what they were.

John Galsworthy (1867–1933) was born into precisely the kind of family he wrote about — prosperous, professional, property-owning, respectable. Meeting Joseph Conrad on a voyage to the Far East in 1893, and falling in love with the wife of a cousin, were the two events that decisively shaped his literary life. Ada Pearson, later Ada Galsworthy, was his companion for decades before they could marry; the experience of that irregular relationship gave him the inside knowledge of respectable society's hypocrisies that animates the Forsyte novels.

Galsworthy received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1932, the year before his death. On Forsyte 'Change appeared two years before the Prize, adding a coda to a literary achievement whose sustained quality and moral seriousness had made it central to the Edwardian and interwar literary landscape.

That two Galsworthy titles appear in this library — On Forsyte 'Change (1930) and The Man of Property (1935) — suggests consistent admiration. The two are best understood together: the novel as the central achievement, the stories as the affectionate annexe to a world Galsworthy had created over thirty years and was reluctant to leave.
contents: Stories of the elder Forsytes: Old Jolyon, James, Timothy, and the generation before Soames
Irene and Bosinney: the affair at the heart of The Man of Property, revisited in shorter compass
Young Jolyon's world: art, bohemianism, and the Forsyte who escaped the family property sense
Jon and Fleur: the younger generation's doomed romance across the Forsyte-Irene divide
Twilight sketches: the Forsyte family in old age, dispersal, and the aftermath of the Great War

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Fourth — Catalogue No. XLIV
books.index_title: Modern Poetry — An Anthology 1922–1934
books.author: Ed. Guy Pocock
subtitle_lines: An Anthology
books.imprint: Published by J. M. Dent and Sons — London, MDCCCXXXII. Everyman's Library
essay: Guy Pocock's anthology Modern Poetry, published in 1932 in Dent's Everyman's Library, gathered work from across the 1920s and early 1930s — a period that produced, alongside the high modernism of Eliot and Pound, a rich body of more accessible work that received rather less critical attention and rather more readers. The anthology's scope reflects the editorial sensibility of a man who wished to represent the period's poetry to a general readership rather than to academics.

The 1920s were a period of violent literary disagreement about what poetry was and what it was for. The Imagists, the Symbolists, and the Modernists had declared war on Victorian conventions; the Georgian poets offered a quieter alternative; and the war poets — Owen, Sassoon, Rosenberg, Graves — forced a reckoning with subject matter neither party had anticipated. By 1932, when Pocock compiled his anthology, several traditions had survived the upheaval.

Dent's Everyman's Library, in which this anthology appeared, was one of the great Victorian and Edwardian democratic publishing initiatives — a series founded in 1906 to make the world's great literature available to working-class readers at an affordable price. By 1932, the series had expanded to include contemporary work alongside the classics.

Guy Pocock (1880–1955) was an editor at Dent whose work on the Everyman's Library shaped the reading habits of several generations. He edited anthologies of verse and prose across many decades, with the conviction that good poetry, properly selected, could reach any educated reader. His instinct was always for work that earned its effects by emotional and imaginative truth rather than theoretical novelty.

To read an anthology of 'modern poetry' published in 1932 is to encounter the future from a particular angle: the poets who appeared contemporary to Pocock have since been divided by history into the canonical and the forgotten. The anthology preserves a moment before those judgements were made, when all its contributors were simply contemporary poets doing their work in real time.
contents: Selection from Georgian poetry: de la Mare, Masefield, Davies, and the tradition of lyric accessibility
War poetry and its aftermath: the continuing influence of Owen, Sassoon, and Graves
The new formalists: poets working within traditional metres but with modern sensibility
Selections from Irish poetry: Yeats's later work and the poets of the Revival's second generation
Editorial note on principles of selection and a brief account of the decade's poetic movements

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Fifth — Catalogue No. XLV
books.index_title: The Life of Samuel Johnson — Volume I
books.author: James Boswell
subtitle_lines: Volume the First
books.imprint: Published 1933 edition
essay: Boswell's Life of Johnson is the greatest biography in the English language and one of the most pleasurable long books ever written. Published in 1791, eleven years after Johnson's death, the writing of it had occupied Boswell for almost the whole of the intervening period. The book is 1,300 pages in most modern editions, dense with quoted conversation, letters, anecdotes, and observations. It is also the fullest self-portrait of a biographer in the literature: Boswell is present on almost every page, arguing with his subject, worrying about his own worth, and recording everything with an almost clinical attention that has no predecessor and no true successor.

James Boswell (1740–1795) first met Samuel Johnson in May 1763, in the back parlour of Thomas Davies's bookshop in Russell Street, Covent Garden. Boswell was twenty-two, Johnson was fifty-three. The encounter was unpromising — Johnson initially dismissive, Boswell nervously ingratiating — but it initiated one of the great literary friendships, sustained over twenty-one years of intermittent meeting, extensive correspondence, and Boswell's systematic recording of Johnson's conversation.

The result is a Johnson who is more fully alive on the page than almost any other figure in literary history: the enormous physical bulk, the convulsive nervous tics, the explosions of prejudice and the sudden reversals of generosity, the terror of death and the massive moral courage, the affection for cats and orange peel. Boswell caught not a statue but a man, and the man he caught was one of the most interesting ever produced by the English language.

Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) was the son of a Lichfield bookseller, educated at Oxford but unable to take his degree for lack of money, and employed for years as a literary hack before being recognised as the dominant literary intelligence of his age. The Dictionary of the English Language (1755), which he compiled largely alone over nine years, is the monument of his scholarship. But it is Boswell who made him immortal.

Volume I covers Johnson's life from his birth in 1709 to approximately 1763 — the period before Boswell met him, which Boswell reconstructed from documentary evidence and the testimony of others. It includes the Lichfield childhood, the Oxford years, the long London struggle, the Dictionary, and the Royal pension that in 1762 finally freed Johnson from financial anxiety.
contents: The Lichfield childhood: Johnson's father, his early reading, and the scrofula that marked his body
Oxford and after: one year at Pembroke College, departure for want of money, and the years of obscurity
The Dictionary: nine years of largely solitary labour, producing the first great English lexicon
The pension of 1762: Royal recognition, financial relief, and the meeting with Boswell
Johnson's circle: Burke, Reynolds, Goldsmith, Garrick, and the founding of the Literary Club

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Sixth — Catalogue No. XLVI
books.index_title: The Life of Samuel Johnson — Volume II
books.author: James Boswell
subtitle_lines: Volume the Second
books.imprint: Published 1933 edition
essay: Volume II picks up the story at the meeting in Davies's bookshop in May 1763 and carries it through to Johnson's death on 13 December 1784. It is the fuller volume in every sense: Boswell was present for most of what it records, and the quality of his observation is at its most acute. The great journeys are here — the Hebrides tour of 1773 — as are the Literary Club conversations, the quarrels and reconciliations, the anxious letters about immortality, and the final illness in Bolt Court.

The conversations recorded in Volume II are among the most quoted passages in English prose. Johnson on women preaching: 'Sir, a woman's preaching is like a dog's walking on his hinder legs. It is not done well; but you are surprized to find it done at all.' Johnson on Scotland: 'the noblest prospect which a Scotchman ever sees is the high road that leads him to England.' The justice of these comparisons remains disputed.

Boswell's great achievement in these later sections is the maintenance of dramatic variety across such a vast canvas. Johnson's age and failing health give the later chapters an elegiac quality, but Boswell never allows sentiment to become sentimentality. The final illness — the dropsy, the asthma, the fear that he has not made sufficient preparation for death — is rendered with the same precision and the same affection that characterises the whole.

The Life was received immediately as a masterpiece. Edmond Malone, who had helped Boswell with the final preparation of the manuscript, called it the most entertaining book he had ever read. The only significant dissent came from Mrs Piozzi (Hester Lynch Thrale), whose own Anecdotes of the Late Samuel Johnson had appeared in 1786 and who resented Boswell's implicit claim to superior knowledge of the man.

James Boswell died in 1795, four years after the publication of the Life. His journals, discovered in the 1920s in remarkable caches at Malahide Castle in Ireland and at Fettercairn House in Scotland, revealed a Boswell more complex and more self-aware than the eager sycophant that some readers of the Life had imagined. The journals and the Life together constitute one of the great self-portraits in any literature.
contents: The Boswell-Johnson friendship: its terms, its tensions, and its extraordinary productivity
The Hebrides tour of 1773: Johnson and Boswell in Scotland — a journey through time as much as space
The Literary Club: Burke, Reynolds, Goldsmith, Garrick, and the conversations recorded in full
Johnson's religion: his terror of death, his prayers, and his complicated relationship with orthodoxy
The final illness and death: Bolt Court, 13 December 1784 — 'I am moriturus'

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Seventh — Catalogue No. XLVII
books.index_title: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby
books.author: Charles Dickens
title_lines: The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby
books.imprint: Published 1935 edition
essay: Nicholas Nickleby was published in twenty monthly parts between April 1838 and October 1839, Dickens's third novel and the one in which his characteristic energies first fully declared themselves. The Yorkshire schools — Dotheboys Hall, Squeers, and Smike — gave the book its moral centre and its most enduring characters; but the novel as a whole is a wonderfully crowded, digressive, improvisatory work, full of theatrical sub-plots, comic grotesques, and the kind of sustained invention that suggests an author barely keeping up with the material pouring from him.

Dickens visited the Yorkshire schools himself in January 1838, travelling with his illustrator Phiz in the depths of winter under a false identity. What he found was worse than he had anticipated: boys sent north by parents who wished to forget them, receiving minimal education and brutal treatment. Wackford Squeers and his family are caricatures, but caricatures built on observed reality. The Yorkshire schools were closed within years of the novel's publication.

Smike — the broken, bewildered creature whom Nicholas rescues from Dotheboys Hall and who never quite recovers — is the emotional centre of the book. His parentage, gradually revealed, provides the novel's principal plot mystery; his death provides its deepest pathos. Dickens rendered damaged children with a conviction that came partly from observation and partly from a more personal source: his own childhood experience of factory work, which haunted his fiction from beginning to end.

Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was born in Portsmouth. His father's improvidence led the family into debt and eventually into the Marshalsea Prison for debtors. The twelve-year-old Dickens was sent to work in a blacking warehouse. He never forgot the experience or entirely forgave his parents for it. His novels return obsessively to the vulnerability of children in the face of adult cruelty and institutional indifference.

The 1935 edition is one of many reprints that kept Dickens's novels continuously in print through the twentieth century. Nicholas Nickleby is not the most perfectly constructed of his novels — the theatrical Crummles sub-plots have been called distracting — but it has a vitality and generosity that make it irresistible, and a freshness that belongs to a young writer discovering his powers.
contents: Dotheboys Hall: Squeers, Smike, and the exposure of the Yorkshire schools
The Crummles theatrical company: a world of professional make-believe and genuine affection
The Cheeryble brothers: commerce as benevolence — Dickens's most optimistic businessmen
Ralph Nickleby: usury, self-interest, and the uncle who persecutes his own nephew
Smike's parentage revealed: the plot's secret and the novel's deepest pathos

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Eighth — Catalogue No. XLVIII
books.index_title: Cakes and Ale; or, The Skeleton in the Cupboard
books.author: W. Somerset Maugham
subtitle_lines: or, The Skeleton in the Cupboard
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, 1935 edition
essay: Cakes and Ale was published in 1930 and is generally considered Somerset Maugham's finest novel — the book in which his wit, his powers of observation, and his emotional honesty are most perfectly integrated. It is narrated by William Ashenden (Maugham's recurring autobiographical alter ego) and concerns his memories of the celebrated novelist Edward Driffield and Driffield's first wife Rosie — disreputable by conventional standards and, by Ashenden's, the most naturally generous human being he ever knew.

The satirical target was identified at once: Driffield bore a suspicious resemblance to Thomas Hardy, and the portrait of the novelist elevated to Grand Old Man — visited by the literary establishment, managed by his second wife, his early disreputable life carefully suppressed — had a precision that suggested specific models. Hugh Walpole, also recognisable in the depiction of the socially ambitious literary man Alroy Kear, was furious. Maugham denied the resemblances, unconvincingly.

Rosie Driffield is one of the most original creations in twentieth-century English fiction: a barmaid who married an unsuccessful novelist, was unfaithful to him with a cheerful generosity that never constituted betrayal, and exits the novel for Canada with a coal merchant, apparently content. She gives pleasure and receives it, without cruelty, without calculation, and without the self-serving respectability that corrupts everyone else in the book.

W. Somerset Maugham (1874–1965) was born in Paris, orphaned young, sent to England to live with an uncle in Whitstable — the model for Blackstable in Of Human Bondage and Cakes and Ale. He studied medicine, qualified, and never practised. He became the most commercially successful English novelist of the first half of the twentieth century and one of the most technically accomplished writers of short fiction in any language.

The title comes from Twelfth Night: 'Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?' It is the perfect epigraph for a novel that defends, against the claims of respectability and self-importance, the older tradition of pleasure, generosity, and the refusal to pretend to be better than you are.
contents: Edward Driffield: the Grand Old Man of English letters, and what his elevation conceals
Rosie: the barmaid, the first wife, the most generous human being in the novel
Alroy Kear: the social-climbing literary man and his ambitions for Driffield's posthumous reputation
Blackstable memories: Ashenden's childhood and his first encounter with Driffield and Rosie
The literary establishment satirised: how fame is manufactured and the inconvenient past suppressed

books.eyebrow: Entry the Forty-Ninth — Catalogue No. XLIX
books.index_title: Poor Jack
books.author: Captain Frederick Marryat
books.imprint: Published 1935 edition
essay: Poor Jack was published in 1840, one of the later novels of Captain Frederick Marryat, set among the watermen and oyster-catchers of the Thames estuary — the world of Gravesend, the Medway, and the lower reaches of the river that Marryat knew from his early naval service. It is a more sentimental and less vigorous book than his great sea novels — Mr Midshipman Easy (1836) and Snarleyyow (1837) — sometimes described as a tale for children, though its picture of estuarial life gives it a documentary interest that transcends the genre.

The story follows Jack Saunders, son of a Thames waterman, from childhood through adolescence and early manhood, tracking his moral development against the background of the river and its occupants. Marryat's Thames is a world of considerable human variety: watermen, smugglers, excise officers, fishwives, naval officers, and the oyster trade, all rendered with the sharp observation of a man who had spent his professional life at sea.

Frederick Marryat (1792–1848) went to sea at fourteen, served under the great frigate captain Thomas Cochrane (the original of Patrick O'Brian's Jack Aubrey and C. S. Forester's Hornblower), and retired from the Navy in 1830 with the rank of captain and a CB. He had already begun writing fiction during his naval service, and after retirement produced a novel a year. His naval novels created the template for the genre and influenced every subsequent writer in the tradition.

Poor Jack belongs to Marryat's later period, when he had left the naval world of his great early novels and was exploring other material. It lacks the pace and comedy of Midshipman Easy, but it has a gentleness and a genuine feeling for the lives of working people on the river. The Thames setting is rendered with affectionate precision.

As a novelist of the sea and the maritime world, Marryat occupies the position of a founding ancestor — not the greatest practitioner in the tradition, but the man who established its possibilities. Patrick O'Brian, Conrad, and Kipling all acknowledged their debt to him explicitly.
contents: Jack Saunders's childhood: the Thames estuary, his waterman father, and early moral formation
The watermen's world: oyster-catchers, smugglers, and the complicated economy of the lower Thames
The river as character: tides, weather, and the human life sustained by the estuary
Marryat's Thames compared to his naval novels: a quieter canvas, more domestic in scale
The didactic thread: honesty, courage, and the making of a good man in a difficult world

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fiftieth — Catalogue No. L
books.index_title: Gallions Reach
books.author: H. M. Tomlinson
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, 1935 edition
essay: Gallions Reach was published in 1927 and is Henry Major Tomlinson's finest novel — a work that sits at the intersection of adventure story, philosophical meditation, and impressionist prose poem. The title refers to the reach of the Thames below the Royal Albert Dock, the last sight of England for a man shipping out from London: departure, the point of no return, the threshold between the known world and everything beyond it.

The plot sends Jim Colet — a shipping clerk who has killed a man in a dockside brawl and fled London — first to the East Indies and then deeper into the Malay jungle, where he is overtaken by fever and by the recognition that whatever he ran from he has carried with him. Tomlinson is less interested in the mechanics of adventure than in the quality of perception: the way the tropics alter consciousness, the way the jungle imposes its own temporality, the way suffering strips away the accretions of civilised self-protection.

Henry Major Tomlinson (1873–1958) was a journalist before he was a novelist — a fact that shows in his prose, which has the vivid immediacy of a man trained to observe and report. He had sailed as a clerk on a small tramp steamer up the Amazon in 1909 and written about it in The Sea and the Jungle (1912), one of the best accounts of equatorial river travel in the language. During the Great War he served as a war correspondent.

Gallions Reach belongs to the inter-war literature of disillusionment. Tomlinson's response was not satire or anger but a kind of lyrical withdrawal into the qualities of particular experience: the sound of a ship's engines, the colour of river water at different hours, the specific smell of a tropical port. His faith, if he had one, was in the reality of immediate sensation and the possibility of seeing truly, without the distorting lens of received ideas.

The 1935 edition is one of several reprints of a novel that enjoyed considerable critical esteem in the 1920s and 1930s, before Tomlinson was largely forgotten by the post-war literary world. He is a writer who rewards rediscovery: his prose, at its best, has a quality of attention that puts him in the company of Richard Jefferies and Edward Thomas among English writers for whom the visible world is both sufficient and inexhaustible.
contents: Gallions Reach: the tidal Thames below the docks — departure and the point of no return
Jim Colet's flight: a dockside killing, a ship, and the impossibility of escaping oneself
The East Indies: the tropics as both physical reality and psychological testing ground
The Malay jungle: fever, time distorted, and the dissolution of the civilised self
The prose: Tomlinson's impressionist style — immediate, sensory, and deeply indebted to Conrad

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-First — Catalogue No. LI
books.index_title: Without My Cloak
books.author: Kate O'Brien
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, 1935 edition
essay: Without My Cloak was Kate O'Brien's first novel, published in 1931, winning both the Hawthornden Prize and the James Tait Black Memorial Prize — a double achievement no first novel had previously accomplished. It is a large-scale family chronicle, set in the prosperous Catholic merchant class of Mellick (Limerick) from the 1830s to the 1890s, establishing O'Brien immediately as a novelist of European seriousness — a writer in the tradition of Flaubert and Stendhal who happened to be Irish.

The novel follows the Considine family across three generations: Anthony Considine, the self-made founder; Honest John, a man of deep conventional decency; and Honest John's son Denis, who becomes the central consciousness and central problem. Denis is rich, handsome, charming, beloved — and incapable of the marital happiness his family expects. His deepest attachment is to his cousin Corney, a relationship the novel does not name but treats with sympathy and precision that makes the constraint perfectly legible.

Kate O'Brien (1897–1974) was born in Limerick, the daughter of a prosperous Catholic horse-dealing family. She was educated at Laurel Hill Convent and University College Dublin, then worked as a journalist and governess in England, Spain, and America before her first play was produced in 1926. Spain became the second great subject of her fiction alongside the Catholic bourgeois Ireland she had left behind.

Without My Cloak is the foundation of O'Brien's achievement: the novel in which she establishes the milieu, the moral framework, and the emotional concerns that she would return to throughout her career. The Considine world — its Catholicism, its commercial success, its carefully maintained respectability, and the powerful feelings that respectability barely contains — is rendered with the combination of affection and clear-eyed analysis that marks the best provincial fiction.

That a Kate O'Brien novel should appear in this library requires no explanation: she is an Irish novelist of the first rank, born in the same prosperous Catholic provincial culture that the library's owner would have recognised, and writing about it with a European seriousness that sets her apart from all her contemporaries. Without My Cloak is the best place to begin with her work.
contents: Anthony Considine: the self-made merchant founder and the Considine family's Mellick world
Honest John: conventional decency, commercial success, and the generous limitations of the bourgeois father
Denis Considine: charm, wealth, unhappy marriage, and the attachment to Corney he cannot name
The Catholic merchant world of Mellick: its domestic life, its respectability, and its constraints
The European tradition: O'Brien's debt to Flaubert and Stendhal in her treatment of provincial society

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Second — Catalogue No. LII
books.index_title: Angel Pavement
books.author: J. B. Priestley
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, 1935 edition
essay: Angel Pavement was published in 1930, the year after The Good Companions had made Priestley famous, and is a darker and more accomplished novel. It is a study of a small London business — Twigg and Dersingham, dealers in inlaid woods and veneers — and the effect upon its employees of a charismatic stranger who offers the firm a lucrative new arrangement and destroys them all. It is Priestley's most Dickensian novel, and his most morally serious.

The London of Angel Pavement is the London of the Depression years — a city of grey offices, threadbare respectability, and the specific anxiety of clerks and small businessmen who know that the margin between comfort and ruin is very narrow. Priestley renders this world with the same documentary precision that he would bring to the English Journey (1934) a few years later. The title refers to a real dead-end alley in the City of London near London Wall.

J. B. Priestley (1894–1984) was born in Bradford, the son of a schoolteacher, educated at Cambridge after service in the Great War, and established himself in the 1920s as one of the most productive and versatile writers of his generation. He wrote novels, plays, travel books, criticism, and essays with a fluency and range that some critics found suspicious but that was simply the expression of a powerful and well-organised intelligence.

The arrival of the mysterious Mr Golspie at Twigg and Dersingham's offices sets in motion a plot of considerable ingenuity and moral darkness: Golspie is not quite a villain but is entirely unscrupulous, and the havoc he creates is the more disturbing for being entirely comprehensible in terms of his own reasonable self-interest. The employees he ruins — the elderly bookkeeper Smeeth, the bored young typist Turgis, the owner Dersingham — are rendered with sympathetic precision.

Angel Pavement was a Book Society Choice on publication and widely regarded as a significant advance on The Good Companions. Priestley was one of the most accomplished and socially alert novelists of the interwar period, and Angel Pavement is the strongest evidence for that claim.
contents: Twigg and Dersingham's: the small City firm, its employees, and its precarious existence
Mr Golspie: the charismatic stranger, his Baltic timber deal, and the disaster he leaves behind
Mr Smeeth: the bookkeeper and the specific anxiety of lower-middle-class respectability
Turgis: the young clerk and his doomed infatuation — romantic longing in a world of offices
London as character: the City's grey afternoons and the geography of urban loneliness

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Third — Catalogue No. LIII
books.index_title: Father and Son — A Study of Two Temperaments
books.author: Edmund Gosse
subtitle_lines: A Study of Two Temperaments
books.imprint: Published 1935 edition
essay: Father and Son was published anonymously in 1907 and is one of the most extraordinary books in the English language — simultaneously a memoir, a study in religious psychology, and a portrait of a relationship so singular that it reads like a novel that happened to be true. Edmund Gosse describes his childhood as the only child of Philip Henry Gosse, the distinguished naturalist and committed Plymouth Brethren minister, and the slow, painful, ultimately liberating process by which he separated his own identity from the totalitarian love his father bore him.

Philip Henry Gosse (1810–1888) was a genuinely remarkable man: a self-taught zoologist whose work on marine invertebrates was of real scientific significance, and the inventor of the marine aquarium. He was also a man of total religious conviction who, when Darwin's Origin of Species threatened the geological record as evidence of divine creation, published Omphalos (1857) — the extraordinary argument that God created the world complete with the appearance of age, fossils and all. The scientific world mocked it; the religious world distrusted it.

Edmund Gosse (1849–1928) grew up in this world of total Evangelical conviction: without art, theatre, or fiction; without the social intercourse that might have moderated the intensity of the father-son relationship; with only the Bible, the meetings of the Brethren, and the studies of marine life. The child accepted this world as the only possible one; the young man began, slowly and guiltily, to suspect that other worlds existed.

The book's literary quality has sometimes been disputed — labelled fiction by some reviewers. But the moral courage of it is beyond dispute: to describe one's own religious liberation in terms that make it comprehensible without vindictiveness toward the father who imposed the original constraint required a precision of self-knowledge and a generosity of spirit that few autobiographers have managed. Gosse manages both.

Father and Son belongs to a tradition of Victorian and Edwardian accounts of religious loss — Samuel Butler's The Way of All Flesh, Leslie Stephen's essays, Matthew Arnold's poetry — in which the children of Evangelical households describe, with varying degrees of grief and relief, the process of intellectual emancipation. Gosse's account is the most personal and the most precise, and it has lasted best.
contents: Philip Gosse: the naturalist, the Plymouth Brother, and the author of Omphalos
Childhood in the Brethren: a world without art, theatre, or fiction — only Scripture and marine specimens
The crisis of adolescence: theatre, poetry, and the first trembling of another world
The final separation: Gosse's departure from his father's faith and the grief of both parties
Two temperaments: the Evangelical absolutist and the literary humanist — a study in irreconcilable love

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Fourth — Catalogue No. LIV
books.index_title: Confessions of a Young Man
books.author: George Moore
books.imprint: Published 1935 edition
essay: Confessions of a Young Man was first published in 1888, the record of George Moore's decade in Paris during the 1870s and early 1880s — his years as a student painter, his encounters with the Impressionists, his discovery of Zola and the French Naturalists, and his gradual conversion from painting to writing. It is the most vivid account of artistic Paris in the period of Manet, Degas, and Renoir, written by a man who was present at the creation of modernism.

Moore arrived in Paris in 1873 with a small income from his Irish estates and enormous ambitions as a painter. He attended the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and spent years in the cafes of Montmartre before acknowledging that he would never be more than a mediocre painter. The discovery of Zola's L'Assommoir in 1877 redirected him toward fiction: he read it in a single sitting in a cafe on the Boulevard des Italiens and recognised immediately that this was what he wished to do.

George Moore (1852–1933) was born at Moore Hall in County Mayo, the eldest son of a Catholic landowner. His years in Paris were financed by the rents from his Mayo estate, paid by tenants simultaneously impoverished by the agricultural depression of the 1870s and organising under Davitt's Land League. Moore was aware of the irony and felt it with some discomfort.

The Confessions is written in a style that is itself a performance of the aesthetic values it advocates: sinuous, self-conscious, frankly concerned with the quality of its own prose, and indifferent to the moral judgements that Victorian readers expected from any account of Bohemian life. It is a portrait of an education — in how to look and feel as much as in how to write.

Moore returned to Ireland in the 1890s, collaborated with Yeats and Lady Gregory on the Abbey Theatre, and then — irritated by the provincialism of the revivalists — settled in London. The Confessions, reprinted many times, remained the book that introduced English readers to the world of French Impressionism and to the aesthetic philosophy that underlay it.
contents: Paris in the 1870s: the Impressionists, the Naturalists, and the cafes of Montmartre
The failure of painting: Moore's honest reckoning with his own mediocrity as a visual artist
The discovery of Zola: L'Assommoir and the conversion to fiction
The aesthetic philosophy: the primacy of sensation, the independence of art from morality
Return to England: bringing French literary values to a Victorian literary establishment

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Fifth — Catalogue No. LV
books.index_title: The Man of Property
books.author: John Galsworthy
subtitle_lines: Being the First Part of The Forsyte Saga
books.imprint: Published by William Heinemann — London, 1935 edition
essay: The Man of Property was published in 1906 and is the finest of Galsworthy's novels. At its centre is Soames Forsyte's marriage to Irene, his sexual claim over a woman who has ceased to love him, and his building of a house at Robin Hill — designed by the architect Bosinney, with whom Irene falls in love. The collision between Soames's property sense and Irene's human freedom, expressed through the house and the marriage, is one of the most precise studies of male possession in Edwardian fiction.

Galsworthy's method is ironic: he presents the Forsyte world from inside, with full sympathy for its values and its people, while making clear that those values are inadequate to the human reality they attempt to contain. Soames is not a villain; he is a man whose emotional life has been entirely converted into the language of ownership, so that he cannot conceive of Irene's freedom as legitimate. His legal right to her body — which the novel treats with deliberate understatement — is the property sense applied to a human being.

Irene herself is the novel's most problematic creation: she is defined almost entirely by what others feel about her, and has almost no interiority of her own. This is either a structural weakness or a deliberate formal choice. Galsworthy may have intended her opacity as a formal expression of her unknowability — she is what Soames cannot possess, cannot know, cannot contain.

John Galsworthy (1867–1933) began the Forsyte Saga in 1906 and returned to it for sixteen years, completing the trilogy with In Chancery (1920) and To Let (1921). The Saga was republished as a single volume in 1922 and became one of the best-selling works of the interwar period. Galsworthy received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1932. He died in January 1933, a month after receiving the Prize, without travelling to Stockholm.

The Man of Property remains the most enduring product of Edwardian fiction's engagement with the property-owning classes — the novel that most fully dramatised what it cost to live in a world where everything, including people, was convertible into permanent holdings.
contents: The Forsyte family: their extent, their unity, their shared property sense — old Jolyon's dinner party
Soames and Irene: the marriage, the estrangement, and the legal reality of possession
Robin Hill: the house as the material expression of Soames's claim over Irene
Bosinney: the architect, his relationship with Irene, and his destruction by the Forsyte world
The property sense: Galsworthy's central theme — the conversion of human beings into things that can be owned

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Sixth — Catalogue No. LVI
books.index_title: Cuchulain of Muirthemne
books.author: Lady Gregory
subtitle_lines: The Story of the Men of the Red Branch of Ulster
edition_lines: Arranged and Put into English by Lady Gregory
books.imprint: Published by John Murray — London, 1937 edition. With a Preface by W. B. Yeats
essay: Cuchulain of Muirthemne was published in 1902 and is Lady Gregory's masterwork — a retelling of the Ulster Cycle, the great body of Old and Middle Irish heroic narratives, in the Kiltartan English of Connacht speech. The book gathers the stories of the Red Branch warriors — Cuchulain, Fergus, Conall Cearnach, Deirdre and the Sons of Uisneach — from manuscripts scattered across European libraries and renders them in a prose that is simultaneously scholarly and literary. Yeats, in his preface, called it the best book that had come out of Ireland in his time.

The figure of Cuchulain — the champion of Ulster, the warrior whose fatal flaw is the geis that compels him to fight against impossible odds — became for Yeats the emblem of heroic defiance, the man who dies magnificently rather than lives compromisingly. Yeats returned to the material throughout his career, writing five plays about Cuchulain from On Baile's Strand (1904) to The Death of Cuchulain (1939).

Lady Augusta Gregory (1852–1932) was born Augusta Persse in County Galway, married Sir William Gregory of Coole Park, and after his death devoted her formidable energies to the Irish literary revival. She co-founded the Abbey Theatre with Yeats and Edward Martyn, managed it for decades, and wrote dozens of plays. Her translations from Irish mythology — Cuchulain of Muirthemne and Gods and Fighting Men (1904) — provided the revival with its mythological foundation.

The Kiltartan prose style — named after the Kiltartan crossroads near Coole — was Lady Gregory's great creative invention: a literary language that reproduced the cadences of Irish-English speech without either condescending to them or rendering them as exotic curiosity. It is the language of people who are simultaneously thinking in Irish and speaking in English — a heightened vernacular that becomes the vehicle for heroic narrative of the highest seriousness.

The 1937 edition is one of several reprints of a book that has never gone out of print since 1902. Cuchulain of Muirthemne is to Irish mythology what the Mabinogion is to Welsh mythology: the first modern literary rendering of an ancient tradition that makes it available to readers who cannot approach the original texts. Its influence on Irish literature — on Yeats above all — cannot be overstated.
contents: The Birth of Cuchulain: his divine parentage and his coming to the Red Branch
The Cattle Raid of Cooley: Ulster against Connacht and Cuchulain's single combat
Deirdre and the Sons of Uisneach: the greatest tragic love story in the Irish tradition
The Death of Cuchulain: betrayal, the standing fight, and the hero's end
The Kiltartan style: Lady Gregory's English voice for Irish heroic narrative

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Seventh — Catalogue No. LVII
books.index_title: Le Vicomte de Bragelonne
books.author: Alexandre Dumas
subtitle_lines: ou Dix Ans Plus Tard
books.imprint: Published 1940 edition
essay: Le Vicomte de Bragelonne is the third and longest of Dumas's Musketeers novels, published in serial form between 1847 and 1850, and in a peculiar literary position: it is less famous than its predecessors but, in its final sections, the most tragic and emotionally ambitious of the three. It contains the Man in the Iron Mask sections — in which Aramis and Porthos attempt to replace Louis XIV with his twin brother — and the story of Raoul, Athos's son, and his doomed love for Louise de la Valliere.

The Man in the Iron Mask sections are by far the best-known part — separately published and separately filmed more times than can be counted. Aramis's plan to substitute the imprisoned twin for Louis XIV is conceived with his characteristic combination of religious vocation and political ruthlessness. Porthos's death in the cave of Locmaria — buried alive by the explosion he himself touches off, too simple and too loyal to understand what has been done to him — is one of the great deaths in popular fiction.

Alexandre Dumas (1802–1870) was born in Villers-Cotterets, the grandson of a Haitian slave and a Norman nobleman. His father, General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, had been one of Napoleon's most gifted commanders. The younger Dumas moved to Paris in 1823 and began writing at a rate of production that gave rise to the persistent legend of a factory of collaborators. The legend is substantially true — Auguste Maquet co-wrote most of the Musketeers novels — but the imaginative force and narrative drive are unmistakably Dumas's own.

The Musketeers trilogy — Les Trois Mousquetaires (1844), Vingt Ans Apres (1845), and Le Vicomte de Bragelonne (1847–50) — is the most sustained feat of popular historical fiction ever accomplished. The final pages, in which d'Artagnan is killed at the siege of Maastricht and Athos dies of grief at the news of Raoul's death in Africa, bring down a world.

A French-language edition of Le Vicomte de Bragelonne in an Irish library of 1940 is partly a testimony to the universality of Dumas's popularity and partly to the French literary culture that educated Irish readers maintained. During the Second World War, Dumas provided exactly what popular historical fiction is supposed to provide: the immediate, total displacement of the reader into another world — one in which the problems, however grave, are resolved by the sword.
contents: The Man in the Iron Mask: Aramis's plot to substitute Louis XIV's twin brother on the throne
Raoul de Bragelonne and Louise de la Valliere: the doomed love story at the heart of the novel
Porthos's death at Locmaria: the most affecting single scene in the Musketeers trilogy
D'Artagnan's final years: the siege of Maastricht and the death of the last Musketeer
Athos's grief and death: the last of the four, dying of a broken heart — an ending of genuine tragedy

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Fifth — Catalogue No. LXV
books.index_title: The Complete Opera Book
books.author: Gustave Kobbé
subtitle_lines: The Stories of the Operas, together with Four Hundred
of the Leading Airs and Motives in Musical Notation
books.imprint: Printed for G. P. Putnam's Sons — New York and London; this reprinting, MCMXLIX
essay: The Complete Opera Book was, for the first half of the twentieth century, the English-speaking world's indispensable companion to the opera house: a fat, friendly volume that retold the plots of the standard repertoire act by act and printed the leading melodies in musical notation so that a reader could pick them out at the piano before going to hear them sung. This is the American edition, reprinted in 1949 — a working book, meant to live on the music-room shelf beside the gramophone rather than behind glass.

The book has one of the more poignant origins in music publishing. Its author, the American critic Gustav Kobbé, had all but finished it when he was killed in 1918 in a genuinely freakish accident: becalmed in his small sailing boat on Long Island's Great South Bay, he was struck and killed by a United States Navy seaplane coming in to land on the water. The manuscript was completed and seen through the press by Katharine Wright, who added a handful of operas of her own marked with her initials, and the book appeared posthumously in 1919 in America and in 1922 in Britain.

What Kobbé offers is not musicology but hospitable enthusiasm. He arranges the operas by composer, walks the reader through each story with a critic's eye and a raconteur's warmth, and studs the text with those four hundred snatches of notation. Read now, it is also a period document: a snapshot of what counted as the operatic canon around 1919 — Wagner and Verdi and Puccini to the fore, the German and Italian mainstream dominant, with the byways of the repertoire treated more briskly. It records a particular moment's taste as faithfully as it records the plots.

Few reference books have outlived their authors so thoroughly. In 1954 the Earl of Harewood revised and greatly expanded it as Kobbé's Complete Opera Book, and in 1997 it was revised again, by Harewood and Antony Peattie, as The New Kobbé's Opera Book — so that a book its author never quite finished has remained in print, under his name, for more than a century. This 1949 American reprint belongs to the last phase of the original 'pure Kobbé' text, before Harewood's hand reshaped it.

It is the one book of music among the literary volumes of this library, and it earns its place precisely as the others do: as an object made to be used and returned to, carrying the marks of a particular civilised pleasure. A opera guide is a curious thing to keep once the performances it describes are long over — but that is rather the point. It preserves not the operas, which need no preserving, but the shape of one enthusiast's delight in them, and the manner in which a whole generation was taught to listen.
contents: Synopses of the standard operatic repertoire, arranged by composer
Four hundred leading airs and motives printed in musical notation
Wagner, Verdi, Puccini and the German and Italian mainstream to the fore
Gustave Kobbé (1857–1918); completed by Katharine Wright after his death
The American edition (G. P. Putnam's Sons), this printing 1949

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Eighth — Catalogue No. LVIII
books.index_title: A Life of the Buddha from a Burmese Manuscript
books.author: Ed. Michael Edwardes
title_lines: A Life of the Buddha from a Burmese Manuscript
books.imprint: Published by The Folio Society — London, MDCCCCLIX
essay: This is a distinctive Folio Society publication, founded in 1947 to produce well-made editions of important texts for a readership that cared about books as physical objects. The Life of the Buddha presented here is drawn from a Burmese manuscript account of the Buddha's life — the tradition of the Theravada Buddhism that spread from India through Burma, Thailand, and Sri Lanka, preserving in Pali and in Burmese vernacular translation an account quite different from the Sanskrit Mahayana tradition that spread north and east into China and Tibet.

Siddhartha Gautama — the historical Buddha — was born, probably in the fifth century BC, in the Shakya republic in what is now southern Nepal. His father was a chieftain of the Shakya clan. The legend of the Four Sights — the old man, the sick man, the corpse, and the renunciant — describes the young prince's first encounter with the reality of suffering, which prompted his abandonment of wife, child, and inheritance to seek liberation. The historical reality behind this legend is disputed, but the narrative has the psychological truth of a profound spiritual autobiography.

Michael Edwardes (1923–1982) was a historian of India and the British Empire whose works include A History of India (1961) and British India 1772–1947 (1967). His editorial work on this Burmese manuscript Life represents a different engagement with Asian civilisation than his historical scholarship: an attempt to make a particular devotional tradition available to Western readers through careful translation and presentation.

The Theravada Life of the Buddha differs from the more familiar northern accounts in its relative austerity: the miraculous elements are present but the emphasis is on the Buddha's humanity, his long searching, and the specific meditative practices by which he achieved enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. The teaching — the Dhamma — is presented as something that can be tested in experience rather than accepted on authority.

A Life of the Buddha in a library that runs from seventeenth-century letters to 1983 naval history is itself a small curiosity — evidence of the breadth of cultivated reading that the twentieth-century Irish educated class maintained. The Folio Society's publication placed it in the hands of readers who might not have sought it out in a more specialist form.
contents: The Four Sights: the old man, the sick man, the corpse, and the renunciant — the prince's awakening
The Great Renunciation: Siddhartha abandons wife, child, and kingdom in search of liberation
The years of austerity: the six-year fast, its failure, and the discovery of the Middle Way
Enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya: the nature of the Buddha's realisation
The First Discourse at Deer Park: the teaching of the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path

books.eyebrow: Entry the Fifty-Ninth — Catalogue No. LIX
books.index_title: The Life of Cardinal Wolsey
books.author: George Cavendish
books.imprint: Published 1962 edition
essay: George Cavendish's Life of Cardinal Wolsey is one of the most valuable historical documents of the Tudor period — the intimate account of Wolsey's rise and fall written by a man who served him as gentleman-usher from 1522 to 1530 and was present at most of the events he describes. Composed in the 1550s and first printed in 1641, it describes what he saw with the honesty and precision of a man who had no axe to grind beyond loyalty to his master's memory.

Cavendish was not a writer by vocation but a servant who happened to witness one of the great dramas of English political history. His Wolsey is neither the omnipotent monster of Protestant polemic nor the idealised statesman of Catholic apology: he is a man of immense ability and worldly ambition who served Henry VIII with absolute fidelity, and was destroyed by his failure to solve the problem — the annulment of Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon — that was ultimately insoluble.

The fall is handled with a dramatic power that Shakespeare drew on directly for his portrait of Wolsey in Henry VIII. The great set-pieces — the surrender of the Great Seal, the journey north, the final illness at Leicester Abbey, and the death-bed speech in which Wolsey reflects that had he served God with half the zeal he served his king he would not have been left to die in shame — have a quality of witnessed reality that no subsequent account has equalled.

George Cavendish (c.1494–c.1562) retired after Wolsey's death to his Suffolk estate, where he spent the remainder of his life and wrote the Life together with a metrical history called Metrical Visions, in which the ghosts of fallen great men describe their downfalls. The prose Life is by far the more important work: the foundation of all subsequent understanding of Wolsey's personality and of the dynamics of Henry VIII's court in the 1520s.

The 1962 edition of Cavendish's Life places it in the post-war scholarly recovery of Tudor texts — the period when paperback publishing and university presses were making primary historical sources available to non-specialist readers. The Life of Wolsey is not a comfortable book for those who prefer their historical figures unambiguous: Wolsey was venal, authoritarian, and magnificently able, and Cavendish's portrait acknowledges all of this without losing its fundamental sympathy.
contents: Wolsey's rise: the butcher's son from Ipswich who became Lord Chancellor and Cardinal-Legate
The Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520): Wolsey's greatest diplomatic achievement
The great matter: Henry VIII's desire to annul his marriage and Wolsey's failure to deliver
The surrender of the Great Seal and the journey north: disgrace and the reality of fallen power
Death at Leicester Abbey, November 1530: the death-bed speech and Cavendish's elegy for his master

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixtieth — Catalogue No. LX
books.index_title: The Wreck of the Wager
books.author: Christopher Hibbert
books.imprint: Published by The Folio Society — London, MDCCCCLXXXIII
essay: The wreck of HMS Wager in May 1741 is one of the great disaster stories in the history of the Royal Navy — a tale of shipwreck, mutiny, murder, and extraordinary survival that gripped the reading public for a generation and had lasting consequences for naval law. Wager was a store ship in Commodore George Anson's squadron; separated from it in the appalling weather off Cape Horn, she struck the rocks of an uninhabited island on the coast of Chilean Patagonia. Of the 120 men who left England with her, barely a dozen would eventually return.

The events on Wager Island after the wreck were as extraordinary as the wreck itself. Captain David Cheap maintained that naval discipline applied regardless of the loss of the ship; most of his men maintained that their service had ended with the sinking. After weeks of mounting tension, Cheap shot a midshipman dead; the majority of the crew mutinied, taking the ship's rebuilt longboat — renamed the Speedwell — and setting off on an 8,000-mile voyage around the Horn to Brazil. Cheap and a small loyal party remained on the island, were rescued by Chilean Indians, and found their way back to England by an equally improbable route.

The Wager disaster had consequences beyond its immediate drama. The central legal question — whether seamen remained under naval discipline after the loss of their ship — was resolved by an Act of Parliament in 1748, introduced by Admiral Anson. This Act led directly to the establishment of the Royal Marines as a permanent sea force in 1755. Among the survivors was Midshipman John Byron — grandfather of the poet Lord Byron.

Christopher Hibbert (1924–2008) was among the most prolific and reliable of popular British historians — the author of some fifty books on subjects ranging from the Risorgimento to the life of George III to the history of London. He brought to each subject thorough research, clear narrative, and the biographer's eye for the telling detail. The Wreck of the Wager is characteristic Hibbert: brisk, well-informed, and genuinely exciting.

That this is a Folio Society edition — beautifully produced, illustrated, and bound — places it in excellent company in this library, alongside the Folio Society's Life of the Buddha (1959). The story belongs to the tradition of maritime literature that includes Anson's own Voyage Round the World and, at a further remove, Patrick O'Brian's Aubrey-Maturin novels, the twentieth century's finest fictional tribute to the eighteenth-century Navy.
contents: The storm off Cape Horn: Anson's squadron scattered, and Wager driven onto the Patagonian coast
Wager Island: the wreck, the survivors, and the collapse of naval discipline
Captain Cheap vs. the mutineers: the legal question of whether naval law survived the loss of the ship
The voyage of the Speedwell: 8,000 miles from Patagonia to Brazil, with appalling losses
Consequences: the Act of Parliament, the Royal Marines, and Midshipman Byron's later career

books.eyebrow: Entry the Sixty-Ninth — Catalogue No. LXIX
books.index_title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne
books.author: Gilbert White
title_lines: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne
books.imprint: Published by The Folio Society — London, MDCCCXCIV
essay: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne is one of the most loved books in the English language — continuously in print since its first publication in 1789, with a demonstrable influence on the development of English nature writing, scientific naturalism, and a particular way of attending to the non-human world that might loosely be called ecological consciousness. It consists of letters addressed by Gilbert White to two correspondents: Daines Barrington, a Welsh judge and naturalist, and Thomas Pennant, the great Welsh zoologist.

The letters cover the natural history of Selborne in Hampshire — the village where White was born in 1720, served as curate for most of his adult life, and died in 1793 — with an attention and patience that make them the finest example of resident naturalism: the discipline of watching one small place closely over many years and building up, from accumulated observation, a picture of its life that no brief visit could provide. White watched the swallows return each spring for decades; he tracked the migrations of birds whose seasonal behaviour was then barely understood.

White's scientific contributions were genuine. He was the first to distinguish the chiff-chaff, the willow warbler, and the wood warbler as three separate species. He made observations on bird migration that contributed to the science; and his notes on earthworms anticipated Darwin's Formation of Vegetable Mould (1881) by almost a century. Darwin himself paid tribute. The naturalist's method — patient, local, empirical, and precise — is the method that produced the great tradition of British field naturalism from White to Darwin to Richard Jefferies.

Gilbert White (1720–1793) was educated at Oriel College Oxford, ordained as a curate, and spent the rest of his life in and around Selborne, serving the church, gardening, corresponding with naturalists across Europe, and watching the world he lived in with a quality of attention that was, in the eighteenth century, almost without precedent. The letters were collected and published in 1789, four years before his death, and became immediately and permanently famous.

The Folio Society edition of 1994 — the last book in this library, numbered sixty-nine in the register — is a beautifully made volume, fitting company for the Folio Society's other contributions to this collection: the Life of the Buddha and the Wreck of the Wager. That the library should end with White is, consciously or not, appropriate: a book about patient attention to a single small place, accumulated over a lifetime, sitting well as the final entry in a collection assembled with the same quality of personal interest and informed pleasure.
contents: The letters to Pennant: birds of Selborne — migration, breeding habits, and the three leaf-warblers distinguished
The letters to Barrington: the tortoise Timothy; earthworms; and the naturalist's method explained
The antiquities: the village's Saxon and medieval history; the Priory of Selborne
White's scientific contributions: the separation of chiff-chaff, willow warbler, and wood warbler
The tradition: White's influence on Darwin, Jefferies, and the English nature writing that followed
